articles.title_orig: Taiwan's first two F-16V fighter jets arrive to bolster defences against China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan's first two F-16V fighter jets arrive to bolster defences against China
articles.content_orig:
The United States has delivered two F-16V ⁠Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack by China .
The aircraft, built by US defence contractor Lockheed Martin, are part of an $8bn deal for 66 F-16Vs approved during President Donald Trump’s first term. They landed on Friday following months of delay due to repeated requests from Beijing to the US to stop arming Taiwan .
The jets, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at noon (04:00 GMT) local time. They arrived a week after Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington .
Taiwan is eyeing a rising military threat from Beijing, ⁠which claims the democratically governed island as its own territory.
“Of course we won’t only have delivered these two [F-16Vs] by the end of the year,” Minister of National Defence Wellington Koo said.
The arrival of the planes comes amid growing concern in Taiwan about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming Taipei.
The US is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to ‌defend itself, but the two have no formal diplomatic relations.
Trump said in May, after meeting Xi in Beijing, that he was holding out on a new $14bn package for Taiwan, though he did approve one worth $11bn in December 2025.
Washington has said there has been no ‌change in policy.
“We continue standing with friends ‌and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan,” a US State Department spokesperson said when asked about the delivery.
The F-16Vs, which received an upgrade in 2023, have advanced avionics, weapons and radar systems to better ⁠counter the Chinese air force, including its  J-20 stealth fighters.
However, Washington has been unwilling to provide Taiwan with its most advanced fighters, such as the F-22 or F-35.

articles.title_orig: ‘I couldn’t let everybody else die,’ says hero Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar
articles.title_zh: ‘I couldn’t let everybody else die,’ says hero Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar
articles.content_orig:
Smit Machchhar, the hero Flydubai captain who fought off a savage attack by his copilot , kept fighting because he could not “let everybody else die,” he said in his first public remarks since Wednesday’s suspected hijacking attempt.
“In that moment, I was fighting for my life,” Machchhar told India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was so severely wounded that I had fallen down… at that time, I was thinking what if I don’t get up?”
A horrific mid-air catastrophe on flight FZ 1073 heading to Tel Aviv was averted in a stunning turn of events on Wednesday when passengers bravely rushed into the cockpit and stand-in pilots regained control of the aircraft.
Machchhar was badly injured while trying to fend off the attacker. Images show showed a gruesome scene onboard, with blood splashed across the cockpit and the seriously wounded pilot lying on the floor, his pained face partially covered with a mask.
Machchhar told Modi he was on the ground in cockpit when he realized the plane was going down.
“And I knew in that moment – one last push, Smit! Just do it. The door is right there,” he said. “And even at that time, he was beating me up.”
“And then I just opened it… and then everybody came,” he said, referring to several other passengers who then rushed into the cockpit and restrained his attacker.
“I was doing this for my life, but at the same time, I knew that I couldn’t let everybody else die.”
Modi praised Machchhar’s heroics, telling the veteran pilot that his “courage, patience and quick thinking… saved the lives of so many people.”
“You yourself were fighting the battle of life and death,” Modi said.
Machchhar is recovering at a hospital in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. He was initially treated for his injuries in Saudi Arabia, where the diverted plane was forced to make an emergency landing.
The father of two had suffered “massive blood loss” and was “severely wounded,” dentist Shota Musaev, a passenger on the flight who helped treat him, previously told CNN.
His bravery “managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told CNN on Wednesday.
Captain Smit Machchhar: The ‘jovial’ pilot and father who thwarted the Flydubai attacker
Machchhar appeared emotional in the call with Modi while recalling the ordeal, and apologized to the Prime Minister for crying on the phone.
The two later spoke in Gujarati, the language predominantly spoken by people from India’s western state of Gujarat, which is where Modi is from.
Machchhar said his daughter had come to see him in hospital but got scared seeing him in his condition. His youngest son, who is two, has not been able to meet him yet, he said.
Born into a family in the textile business, becoming a pilot wasn’t Machchhar’s “childhood dream,” he told the Bona-Fide Banter podcast in 2025. Initially, he’d enrolled in a textile engineering course after school.
Speaking to Modi, Machchhar said he felt a sense of pride.
“Now that you have called me, I am really really proud of myself,” Machchhar said. “I wasn’t proud before this, but now I am.”

articles.title_orig: El Al forced to cancel first rescue flights to Dubai after authorities revoke landing permissions
articles.title_zh: El Al forced to cancel first rescue flights to Dubai after authorities revoke landing permissions
articles.content_orig:
El Al Israel Airlines has been forced to cancel its rescue flights to Dubai , the company announced on Friday morning, after Israeli airlines' permission to land there was revoked by the authorities.
El Al stated that, as soon as official permission is granted for the rescue flights to resume, it would be implementing the planned flights to bring stranded Israelis home.
Meanwhile, the Transportation Ministry said that "following coordination with all relevant parties, it was agreed that flights operated by Israeli airlines from Dubai to Israel would begin on Friday, October 2. However, due to the need to complete the necessary preparations and coordination by security officials for the operation of the flights, a delay is expected in the departure of the repatriation flights from Dubai.
“Citizens currently in Dubai should remain in contact with the airlines through which their tickets were booked and follow their instructions and updates,” the ministry added.
According to estimates, more than 10,000 Israelis are stranded in Dubai and at other destinations from which they had been expected to return to Israel via the United Arab Emirates .
Later on Friday, Israir announced that it had received the final approvals from the Emirati authorities and that flights would be departing from Israel to Dubai during the day. No similar announcement was made by El Al.
On Wednesday, a flydubai aircraft that departed Dubai for Tel Aviv was diverted and landed in Saudi Arabia following an altercation between the captain and the copilot.
During the incident, one of them was stabbed, prompting the activation of the distress signal.
The aircraft initially disappeared from flight tracking systems, raising concerns that it had been hijacked . However, after several tense moments, the circumstances surrounding the incident became clearer, and the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.title_zh: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.content_orig:
Host nation won having led almost from start to finish, while young English player reached a stunning landmark
Uzbekistan, the host nation, won the open gold medals at the 2026 Olympiad, the biennial chess international team tournament, at Samarkand last week in the style of the legendary Soviet grandmasters of long ago. India, the defending champions, were second, Germany a surprise third, and the top-seeded United States fourth.
The hosts led almost from start to finish, with world No 5 Nodirbek Abdusattorov and the world title challenger Javokhir Sindarov their top-board powerhouses. The team recovered swiftly from a single defeat by Germany, and were particularly impressive in crushing Armenia by 3.5-0.5 in the penultimate round. The Uzbekistan government rewarded each of the five players with $200,000 (£178,000), plus $50,000 for the coach Rustam Kasimdzhanov.
India performed in line with their seeding. Putting the world champion, Gukesh Dommaraju, on board four boosted his results but also underlined that Sindarov is the favourite for the coming world championship match. Gukesh was exposed in the final rounds when he was outplayed against both Germany, although he won that game fortuitously, and Hungary.
The final leading scores were: Uzbekistan 20/22 match points; India and Germany 18 ; USA, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Hungary 17 ; China, France, Spain, Ukraine and England 16 (206 teams competed).
England’s creditable 12th place, one below their seeding, would have been still higher if a third player had performed at the level of the nine-time British champion Michael Adams, 54, and the Spectator chess columnist Luke McShane, 42, who were both in contention for individual medals right up to the final round. England’s women were 15th against their seeding of 20th, and the combined performance was the best since at least 2018, and probably since 1990.
Russia/USSR, which monopolised Olympiad golds in the second half of the 20th century, have been banned from the last three competitions due to the invasion of Ukraine. If allowed to take part, a team of Ian Nepomniachtchi, Andrey Esipenko, Daniil Dubov, Vladislav Artemiev and Alexander Grischuk would have been contenders.
The potential of Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus stands out. The 15-year-old won the individual silver medal unbeaten and has advanced to No 17 in the live ratings, a similar level to Bobby Fischer at that age and well ahead of current world No 1 Carlsen when he was 15. Here he defeats a rival prodigy , Argentina’s Faustino Oro.
China won the women’s Olympiad ahead of Kazakhstan, India and the US, and did so with its B team. World champion Ju Wenjun, world No 1 Hou Yifan, former title challenger Tan Zhongyi and world No 3 Lei Tingjie all stayed at home, but their substitutes, led by world No 4 Zhu Jiner and 16-year-old Lu Miaoyi, proved highly effective.
For the future, the US is potentially a powerhouse in women’s chess. Its duo of Carissa Yip, 23, and Alice Lee, 16, are both targeting the open GM title and its $100,000 bonus offered by Dr Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield, while new candidates are emerging in Rachael Li, Rose Atwell and Zoey Tang who are all teenagers with 2300+ ratings.
Bodhana Sivanandan broke the world age record for the youngest ever woman grandmaster (WGM). Her 8/11 total, playing all games with no rest days, included six wins, draws against Ukraine’s reigning European champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn and Georgia’s former World Blitz champion Nana Dzagnidze, both of them current world top 20 players, and a solitary loss to Deysi Cori of Peru due to a time-pressure blunder in a drawn ending.
The 11-year-old Harrow schoolgirl’s record as the youngest ever WGM broke Hou’s 2006 mark by several months, and she also recorded her second norm (of three needed) for the international master (IM) title at open level. For IM, she also needs a 2400 rating against her current 2382, which includes the Olympiad.
Her last-round Olympiad game was a model of what has become her trademark style of a Magnus Carlsen grind.
If she secures her final norm and becomes an IM before her 12th birthday, she will break the all-time female No 1 Judit Polgar’s world age record and also become one of the 10 youngest ever IMs. She is already No 2 among all players born in 2015, behind only Russia’s IM Roman Shogdzhiev, who has been groomed for several years as a potential heir to Anatoly Karpov.

The Guardian’s Matthew Weaver interviewed Sivanandan after her return home. At the end of the Olympiad the youngster talked with Lichess.org’s Theo Wait , while chess.com also covered her achievements in detail .
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s new £250,000 a year Supporting Elite Chess Fund document contains no specific provision for rewarding world-record breakers. Maybe it should, as Sivanandan’s IM title and new record could follow as soon as the London Classic, which begins in November.
Sivanandan has just started at secondary school, and that could slow her progress on the chessboard. The advance from IM to GM is difficult, and many talents eventually plateau, which should temper extrapolations of a rise comparable to Polgar and Hou.
Meanwhile Timur Turlov, 38, a Russian-born entrepreneur from Kazakhstan whose company Freedom Holding has a multibillion dollar valuation on the Nasdaq index, was elected as the new president of the world chess body Fide last Saturday.
The previous Fide President, Russia’s Arkady Dvorkovich, had planned to run for a third term but was forced to withdraw due to EU sanctions on his assets and travel visas.
Turlov received 96 votes against 76 for the German businessman Wadim Rosenstein and a surprisingly low 20 for the ticket of Jan Henric Buettner of Freestyle Chess and the ECF’s international director Malcolm Pein. In the run-off ballot they switched to Turlov, who defeated Rosenstein 110-85.
Turlov is young, committed and with proven business skills. However, there could be an immediate problem since Rosenstein has appealed to the court of arbitration for sport over the new president’s eligibility.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 futures edge higher as September jobs report looms: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 futures edge higher as September jobs report looms: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures inched higher early Friday as traders awaited the release of September's jobs report.
S&P 500 futures were up 0.5%, while futures tied to Dow Jones Industrial Average were up 276 points, or 0.5%. Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.8%.
In the regular trading day, the Dow and the Nasdaq Composite ended the session marginally higher. The S&P 500 posted a 0.2% advance to conclude the first trading day in October. All three indices are on pace for weekly losses, with the Dow off 1.7% in the period.
Treasury yields climbed to multiyear highs before retreating. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield soared to 5.344%, its highest level since 2002. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond also reached its highest in 24 years.
Yields continued to pull back early Friday, trading marginally lower in the early hours of the morning.
It came as oil prices fell sharply on reports that the U.K. and Europe were considering a release of strategic fuel reserves. The Trump administration has pressured European allies to "immediately" release diesel supplies.
Front-month Brent crude oil futures were last seen 2.2% lower at $100.05 per barrel, after dipping below the $100 mark earlier in the day. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures were down by 3.2% to $89.85 a barrel.
Despite volatility in the markets, Luca Paolini, chief strategist at Pictet Asset Management, said he expects global stocks to "power on" thanks to strong earnings momentum.
"After a nine-month rally in equity markets and a recent spike in bond yields, stocks appear expensive relative to fixed income," he said in a Friday morning note. "However, we believe earnings growth remains a more powerful market driver. Companies in the MSCI World index are on track to deliver earnings growth of more than 30% this year, while emerging market firms could see profits rise by over 65%."
September's nonfarm payrolls report will also be in the spotlight Friday, with the Dow Jones consensus calling for job growth of 84,000 and for the unemployment to hold steady at 4.1%.
The report comes as traders reassess the next move for the Federal Reserve. Fed funds futures trading suggests a 72% likelihood the central bank will stand pat in October.
Given that the current narrative suggests the labor market is stable, a strong jobs report alone would likely not push the Fed to hike in October, said Christopher Hodge, a chief U.S. economist at Natixis CIB Americas. Hodge expects growth in the manufacturing and construction sector amid a data center buildout.
"We expect payrolls to slow from the torrid pace from August, but still to register solid gains. We expect payrolls to increase by 60k, which if realized, would bring the three-month moving average of gains to 81k," Hodge said.
Asian stocks closed mixed on Friday. Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 0.94%, while South Korea's Kospi added 0.46%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 traded 0.79% higher. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was 2.8% lower in its last hour of trade. Mainland China markets were closed for a holiday.
European stocks were broadly higher, with the regional Stoxx 600 index rising by almost 1% in early trading.
Moderna will replace Warner Bros. Discovery in the tech-heavy blue-chip Nasdaq 100 index after the biotech's shares have risen nearly sixfold over the past year.
The change will take effect before the market opens on Oct. 9, the stock exchange said in a statement late Thursday.
Shares of Moderna rose 2.4% in premarket trading, adding to a 563% gain over the past 12 months.
The company, which became a household name after it developed one of the first vaccines for Covid-19, surprised the Street last month when an experimental personalized cancer vaccine co-developed with Merck showed positive initial results in its first-ever late-stage trial.
Meanwhile, Warner Bros. is in the process of merging with Paramount Skydance . Paramount has said the merger will close on Oct. 6.
European government bond yields fell on Friday, as they headed for the end of a volatile week that saw yields on various regional securities hit multi-decade highs.
By 9:15 a.m. in London (4:15 a.m. ET), yields on British and German 10-year government bonds were around 7 basis points lower. Their Italian counterparts saw yields move 4 basis points lower, while 10-year bonds issued by France and Switzerland saw yields fall by 2 basis points.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 added 0.3% in early morning trading, with tech stocks leading gains.
Germany's DAX index, up 0.3%, led gains among major regional bourses.
Asian stocks closed mixed on Friday. Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 0.94% to 68,309.46, while the Topix closed 0.99% lower at 4,091.
South Korea's Kospi rose 0.46% to 7,003.74, while the small-cap Kosdaq slid 0.11% to 893.29.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.79% to 8,682.1.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was 2.8% lower in its last hour of trade.
Mainland China markets were closed for a holiday.
Volvo Cars shares are down by more than 5% in premarket trading after the Swedish automaker flagged an increasingly challenging market situation and deteriorating near term outlook, which have hit cash flow and sales volumes.
The group told investors it would not fulfil its previous full-year outlook statements, with lower-than-expected sales and a weaker full year outlook for the company.
"The decline is primarily driven by further deteriorating market conditions in China and slower than expected recovery in the US, while Europe remains resilient," Volvo said.
Brazilians vote on Oct. 4 in the first round of a closely watched presidential election, with incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro dominating the polls.
The result could influence Brazil's relationships with the U.S. and China, including over trade and access to critical minerals, as Bolsonaro emphasizes alignment with Washington while Lula stresses Brazilian sovereignty.
Approximately $1.1 million of the nearly $388 million stolen from crypto exchange Bitget in last week's cyberattack has been frozen, as the platform continues efforts to trace and recover the assets.
Frozen assets had not necessarily been returned to the exchange, CEO Gracy Chen told CNBC in an email interview. She did not disclose how much had been recovered.
Speaking on CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday, Chen said she was "not expecting to recover a lot of funds," citing the limited recovery from previous cryptocurrency exchange hacks. However, "exchanges have a responsibility to demonstrate how they protect users, particularly when something goes wrong," she said.
U.S. Treasury yields rose on Friday, reversing some of the previous session's declines as longer-dated borrowing costs remained near multi-decade highs.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield climbed 1.8 basis points to 5.252%, while the 30-year Treasury yield rose 2.6 basis points to 5.629%.
Treasury yields had eased Thursday after their recent surge, with investors continuing to weigh the outlook for the U.S.-Iran conflict and its potential implications for inflation and interest rates. Yields move inversely to prices.
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has proposed new rules that would make it easier for investment advisers and regulated funds to hold cryptocurrencies on behalf of clients, as U.S. regulators push ahead with writing crypto rules after a sweeping legislation stalled in Congress.
The proposal, announced Thursday stateside, would establish a tailored framework governing how registered investment advisers, investment companies and business development companies hold custody of crypto assets.
The changes are aimed at modernizing decades-old custody requirements and removing regulatory barriers that the SEC says have limited advisers' ability to offer crypto-related investments.

Fresh policy support, falling stocks and rising demand for Chinese bonds shape the week’s market narrative
A sell-off in technology stocks pushed mainland Chinese equities to their lowest level in more than a year, even as Beijing stepped up support for the economy with a key interest rate cut. At the same time, Chinese government bonds attracted fresh interest as US Treasury yields climbed to a new high.
Here are some figures that have captured market attention this week.
Mainland China’s CSI 300 Index dropped 2.2 per cent on Monday to its lowest level since August 21 last year, while the technology-focused Star Market 50 index tumbled 4.1 per cent. A 31 per cent plunge in the Star Market 50 during the third quarter contributed to a 12 per cent decline in the CSI 300.
Mainland Chinese and Hong Kong stocks could face a bumpy road in the fourth quarter amid underwhelming stimulus measures, concerns over further interest rate increases and changing sentiment towards artificial intelligence-related investments, analysts said.
China’s central bank cut the one-year pledged supplementary lending rate to 1.5 per cent from 1.75 per cent on Tuesday, aiming to encourage policy banks to provide funding for projects aligned with national priorities.
The move came alongside a mortgage interest subsidy programme for first-time homebuyers, offering an annualised interest subsidy of 1 percentage point for up to five years for loans with principals of up to 1 million yuan (US$149,000).

Three researchers have been fired from OpenAI after allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization, sources told The Wall Street Journal.
The three researchers worked on the company's safety team, the Journal reported.
"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," an OpenAI spokesperson told the outlet.
"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," the spokesperson added.

The firings come amid heightened scrutiny of AI safety as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has publicly warned about the need to keep increasingly powerful artificial intelligence under human control. (Reuters/Manuel Orbegozo / Reuters Photos)
The firings come as OpenAI and several other major artificial intelligence companies have disclosed incidents involving AI models engaging in unexpected behavior or autonomously accessing other companies' systems.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced last week that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to an Australian government website earlier this year.
The company said there was no evidence that patient records were accessed.
In July, OpenAI disclosed that one of its advanced AI models autonomously hacked into the infrastructure of another AI company, Hugging Face, during internal testing in what it described as an "unprecedented cyber incident ."
Last week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned the United Nations Security Council that rapidly advancing AI could threaten humanity if governments and industry fail to keep it under human control.
MIKE ROWE WARNS US WORKFORCE FACING ‘PROBLEM OF THE DECADE’
OpenAI said it parted ways with three employees for violating company policies governing access to and handling of sensitive information. (Reuters/Dado Ruvic/Illustration / Reuters Photos)
OpenAI has also released information outlining six instances in which its models engaged in what the company described as misaligned behavior.
The company said it found examples of its AI models creating self-generated instructions, concealing mistakes in task summaries, fabricating information using exposed API keys, uploading files to the internet in order to cite them and engaging in unsanctioned communication and collaboration between agents.

FOX Business confirmed earlier this week that OpenAI safety leaders made the decision not to release its new AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, due to safety concerns.
"For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a trade off. You really do need to find what’s the right line between staying within scope, but also avoiding laziness in terms of how the model actually pursues tasks even when it hits friction," Saachi Jain, OpenAI's head of safety systems, said in a statement.
"While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done."
FOX Business has reached out to OpenAI for comment.

articles.title_zh: Not-so-brave new world: virtual taekwondo makes Asian Games debut
articles.content_orig:
Kazakhstan's Rita Bakisheva (R) competes against India's Kashish Malik in the mixed individual virtual taekwondo
Taekwondo dates back more than 2,000 years, but on Friday at the Asian Games the Korean martial art stepped into a not-so-brave future where nobody gets hurt: virtual taekwondo.
At a gymnasium about a 90-minute drive from the main Games host city of Nagoya, a modest number of spectators watched with a mix of fascination and bewilderment.
Taekwondo officials have billed it as "real-world martial arts meets cutting-edge virtual technology".
Competitors wear a VR headset and motion tracking technology allows their movements to control their in-game avatars.
They have "nodes" on their back, thighs and shins to pick up each bodily action.
Rounds are typically 60 seconds each and matches are a best of three rounds, the two combatants standing within their own play area a few metres apart.
The goal is to aim real-life kicks to the virtual body and head of their opponent to deplete their computerised health bar.
The opponent is physically there, standing on an opposing side, but there is never any real-life contact.
Darren Yap won bronze -- to go with another bronze in the traditional format.
"It was fun playing out there. I had zero expectations," said the Singaporean.
Asked what he could see through the VR headset, he said: "You can see your health bar, your opponent's character, your limbs.
"It's actually quite nice to wear.
"It's a fun way to do sparring and it's a fun way to do taekwondo without the contact."
Officials say virtual taekwondo is just as athletically demanding as the real thing, but safer.
Governing body World Taekwondo "proudly endorses" it, calling it "groundbreaking".
Sceptics say it is just another type of gaming.
The first world championships were in 2024 in Singapore, but on Friday it arrived at a bigger stage.
One of the differences to the real-life sport is that men and women compete in a mixed category. There are also no weight classes.
"It allows more people to participate in the sport, and I think it's cool that women are able to beat men," said Yap, 22, after losing his semi-final to Vietnam's woman athlete Chau Ngoc Tuyet Sang.
Singapore has become the early home of the sport. Virtual taekwondo appeared at the inaugural Olympic Esports Week in the city-state in 2023.
Silver medallist Chau, who also competes in the real-life format, had mixed feelings about no gender or weight separation.
"One advantage is that you don't have to worry about the difference in weight," the 21-year-old said.
"But one disadvantage is that men and women can have differences in physical strength, and men may tend to be stronger.
"That could also mean that some of the movements are faster than those performed by women."

articles.title_orig: Trump illegally fired Seattle’s U.S. attorney, judge rules
articles.title_zh: Trump illegally fired Seattle’s U.S. attorney, judge rules
articles.content_orig:
The ruling is the latest in the administration's battle over U.S. attorneys.
A federal judge on Thursday ordered a U.S. attorney from Western Washington who was fired by President Donald Trump in July to immediately be reinstated to the position, and is barring the Justice Department from again attempting to replace him.
The ruling from U.S. District judge Stanley Bastian is the latest escalation in the Trump administration's battle with the judiciary over DOJ efforts to install U.S. attorneys around the country without Senate confirmation.
Federal judges appointed Rogoff to the post that oversees federal prosecutions in Seattle in July, and he was fired by President Trump through an email roughly an hour later.
Rogoff then filed suit citing similar cases around the country where the Trump administration had unsuccessfully sought to install attorneys and extend their service indefinitely, which judges appointed by both parties have ruled clearly violates the appointment statute .
The Justice Department said it disagrees with the decision and plans to appeal and seek a stay.
Judge Bastian ruled from the bench in Thursday's proceeding granting Rogoff's request for a preliminary injunction -- and further enjoined Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Executive Office of the President from taking any further moves to effectuate his termination.

articles.title_orig: Mortgage rates approach 3-year high as new applications plunge
articles.title_zh: Mortgage rates approach 3-year high as new applications plunge
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates keep going up.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% this week, up from 7.03% last week, according to Freddie Mac data released Thursday. Mortgage rates have risen for six straight weeks, and this week brought the biggest one-week jump in nearly four years. Rates are now at their highest level since November 2023.
Turmoil in the bond market is driving rates higher. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen in recent months as investors worry that the Iran war and increased government spending could further stoke inflation and push the Federal Reserve toward higher rates for longer.
If you’re currently in the market for a home, the good news is you may be facing less competition from rate-sensitive buyers who are stepping back. But if you need a mortgage, the bad news is you will likely pay more in monthly costs than you would have just a few months ago.
But even with borrowing costs high – and potentially headed higher – a sub-7% mortgage rate may still be within reach for some buyers. The trade-off could be a riskier loan or a much bigger upfront payment.
Most home buyers opt for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage because it typically offers lower monthly payments and predictable costs.
But it’s not the only option. Other types of mortgages may offer lower interest rates, potentially saving borrowers money over the life of the loan.
A 15-year mortgage typically has a lower interest rate than a 30-year mortgage, though monthly payments are significantly higher. Another option that is becoming increasingly popular lately: adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs).
As of the latest data last week, “ARM loans, with rates around 80 basis points lower than fixed rate loans, accounted for 10.3% of applications, the highest share since October 2025,” according to Joel Kan, deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association.
How are higher interest rates and rising prices affecting you?
But ARM loans, the mortgage products that helped fuel housing market risk in the lead-up to the 2008 financial crisis, are riskier than fixed-rate loans . They typically offer a lower fixed rate for five, seven or 10 years before resetting with market rates. If rates are higher when the fixed period ends, borrowers can be hit with sharply higher monthly payments.
“It may work well for some borrowers who are expecting to move or refinance in four or five years,” said Jeremy Luke, a divisional director at Chase Home Lending. “It may not work for all.”
Another way to get a lower mortgage rate is to take over someone’s existing mortgage as an assumable loan .
Not all home loans can be passed to a home buyer, but most government-backed loans, such as those from the Federal Housing Administration, the US Department of Veterans Affairs and the US Department of Agriculture, are assumable.
However, the approval process for an assumable mortgage can take longer. And because the buyer takes over only the seller’s remaining loan balance, they may need to bring significantly more cash to the table to cover the difference between that balance and the home’s purchase price.
The rate an individual buyer gets depends on more than market conditions. Lenders also consider factors such as the borrower’s credit score, debt-to-income ratio and down payment, said Jeff DerGurahian, head economist at loanDepot.
After shopping around, if you are unsatisfied with the rates you’ve been offered, it’s often possible to pay more up front in exchange for a reduced interest rate.
Permanent buydowns lower your interest rate for the life of the loan, whereas temporary buydowns, which can be cheaper, lower your rate for only the first few years.
But it’s important not to overdo it, DerGurahian said.
“You don’t want to put so much money down that you can’t do what you need to do to live in your house and live day-to-day,” he said.
Sometimes, the home’s seller or a builder can cover the cost of a rate buydown.
Builders are leaning more heavily on incentives to attract buyers to new construction, offering concessions such as mortgage rate buydowns and closing-cost credits. In September, 66% of builders reported using sales incentives, up from 63% in August and the highest share since December, according to the National Association of Home Builders’ sentiment survey.
A buyer should also understand the demand picture in their local market, said DerGurahian.
If it’s a buyer’s market, that means the supply of homes in that area exceeds demand, giving home buyers the upper hand. If a homeowner is motivated to sell, they may be willing to offer concessions to attract a buyer. If sellers have the upper hand in a local market, though, it’s less likely.
Certain buyers may have access to federal programs that can help them secure more favorable mortgage rates, including VA loans for eligible veterans and USDA loans for buyers purchasing homes in qualifying rural areas.
There are also banks and credit unions that offer relationship pricing or preferential rates.
For example, Chase occasionally runs “rate sales” where home buyers (and homeowners looking to refinance) can lock in discounted rates, Luke said.
Some banks, including Chase, also offer a discounted rate if customers move eligible deposits and investments into that bank, Luke added.
It pays to shop around. Experts generally recommend applying with at least three different mortgage lenders to make sure you’re getting a competitive rate. Compare the rates offered, closing costs and other fees to get a clearer picture of the total cost of each loan.
And you don’t necessarily have to worry about multiple credit checks dinging your score. To shop around for mortgages without hurting your credit, limit your search to a window of 14 to 45 days, according to Bankrate.

articles.title_orig: AT&T Acknowledges iPhone 18 Pro Max Issues: 'Update Immediately'
articles.title_zh: AT&T Acknowledges iPhone 18 Pro Max Issues: 'Update Immediately'
articles.content_orig:
In a text message sent to customers today, AT&T acknowledged that some iPhone 18 Pro Max devices on its network are experiencing cellular issues .
AT&T said that customers should immediately update to iOS 27.0.1 , despite the fact that many affected users have said that the update does not resolve the issues. There are now at least thousands of users that have experienced this problem, according to discussion topics across the Apple Support Community , Reddit , and MacRumors Forums .
Here is what the text message says:
Hi, it's AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately — Settings > General > Software Update. Please contact AT&T or Apple if you have questions.
Apple's release notes for iOS 27.0.1 did not mention a fix for AT&T cellular issues. Rather, the update fixed a Face ID issue on the iPhone 18 Pro models.
As we reported last week, affected iPhone 18 Pro Max users are unable to connect to the AT&T network for phone calls, text messages, or data either persistently or intermittently, and their devices typically enter SOS mode as a result. The underlying cause has not been confirmed, and Apple has yet to publicly comment on the matter.
Notably, the U.S. version of the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only new iPhone unveiled last month that is equipped with a Qualcomm cellular modem . The smaller iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo are equipped with Apple's C2 modem worldwide, as is the iPhone 18 Pro Max in all other countries. However, it is unclear if this is a contributing factor.
If a software issue is identified, then another update such as iOS 27.0.2 may be required. If there is a hardware issue, though, then this would obviously be a much bigger problem. We will provide further updates as new information becomes available.
(P.S. There is some irony in AT&T sending a text message to warn iPhone 18 Pro Max users that they might not be able to send or receive text messages.)

articles.title_orig: US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
articles.title_zh: US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
articles.content_orig:
The United States is deploying a third US aircraft carrier to the waters around Iran, a US official told Al Jazeera, as the war enters its eighth month and both sides weigh escalation and diplomatic engagement.
The official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left its San Diego base on Sunday, bound for the region, followed a day later by the Makin Island Marine Expeditionary Force, carrying more than 2,000 Marines.
By the end of November, the official said, three aircraft carriers and two amphibious landing groups will be positioned around Iran.
The official said the concentration of force would hand President Donald Trump a wider menu of options if he decides to act.
Al Jazeera’s Tanya Noury, reporting from Washington, said the new deployment includes thousands of troops and extra air power, including F-35 fighter jets, layered on top of the roughly 50,000 US service members already stationed in the region.
The goal, Noury said, citing sources inside the Pentagon and White House, is to keep military options “on the table” for Trump regardless of how diplomacy unfolds, with the Pentagon not planning to withdraw any assets even if an agreement with Iran is reached. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said forces are “ready to go” should Trump order new strikes.
Trump himself has kept the threat alive in public. He told Fox News he believes the US is “going to win the war” with Iran “very soon”, while suggesting in other remarks that a return to military action “is possible” but something he would rather not spell out before November’s midterm elections.
Washington has paired the show of force with new economic pressure , sanctioning Iran’s rail and automotive conglomerates this week, as the Treasury Department called the new measures an effort to drain what remains of Tehran’s revenue.
Parallel to the military build-up, Iran has pushed a seven-day roadmap , conveyed through Qatar, that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in exchange for an end to the US naval blockade, sanctions relief and a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen.
The plan was then rejected by Trump.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told NBC the plan’s demand for frozen funds and sanctions relief was non-negotiable, noting “these aren’t just the United States’ sanctions … these are global sanctions”, and pointing to seven UN Security Council resolutions against an Iranian nuclear weapons programme.
Iran’s response, in the meantime, has been similarly two-pronged.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC that Tehran was “fully prepared” to resume the war, before writing on X that “we did not come to New York to sell a war. We came to forge peace.”
Analysts say the mixed signals are deliberate.
Abas Aslani of the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies said the dispute has shifted from whether to negotiate to “who is going to abandon the primary leverage first”, while former US ambassador Richard Schmierer said Trump is caught between delaying past the midterms and the political cost of offering concessions that mirror a June deal he was already criticised for.
Nearly 70 percent of Americans now say the war has not been worth fighting , according to a new AP-NORC poll, with Trump brushing off the slide in his approval ratings by insisting “the pollsters are corrupt”.

articles.title_orig: Boeing engineers, tech workers approve contract, avoid strike
articles.title_zh: Boeing engineers, tech workers approve contract, avoid strike
articles.content_orig:
by Jackie Kent, KOMO News Reporter
SEATTLE — Boeing has avoided an engineering strike after more than 17,000 engineers and technical workers on Thursday approved a four-year contract offer promising wage increases and other perks.
The Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace wrapped up its electronic voting at noon.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE | Boeing releases final contract offer to union engineers, technical workers
The bargaining team had recommended members accept the offer as it guarantees a 34% pay boost over four years, including a nearly immediate 10% increase in October. The deal also enhances health care and retirement benefits and adds two vacation days, a new floating holiday, and three bereavement days.
Alex Phillips is a software security engineer for Boeing in Seattle, and he's been fighting for a big pay bump.
"To improve members’ lives and help Boeing do better," Phillips explained. "There’s a lot of things in this contract that I think are stepping stones for making improvements."
Kevin Boyd works out of the Auburn facility as a cutting tool designer, and said it was critical for this contract to increase base salaries.
"I hope this is a foundation we can continue to build a relationship with Boeing," Boyd added.
The agreement means the aerospace company has narrowly avoided a shutdown of engineering development and regulatory compliance at a time when Boeing is under pressure to improve build quality and clear its aircraft backlog.
"The stakes were really high. Certification of the new Boeing 777 and the [Boeing 737] MAX 10 kind of hung in the balance. Those programs surely would’ve been delayed if the engineers and technicians had gone on strike," Leeham News and Analysis Editor Howard Hardee explained. The trade publication and consulting firm tracks Boeing's production struggles, regulatory hurdles and labor relations.
The machinists went on strike for nearly two months in 2024, which hurt the company's bottom line, brought commercial activity across the Puget Sound area to a standstill and hurt efforts to ramp up production rates for the 737 MAX program. Hardee said that's what Boeing wanted to avoid happening again in this round of negotiations.
"Generally speaking, [Boeing has] had  series of wins. They got the MAX 7 certified," Hardee stated. "They have had a setback on certification of the MAX 10, but getting this negotiation process behind them I think is a really positive development for Boeing, and for people watching the industry it can only be a good sign of their continued recovery."
The company has said these final amounts are $11,000 more for professional employees and $8,000 more for technical workers than under its initial offer, which the union rejected in August.
Following the vote to approve the contract offers, Boeing issued this statement:
“We’re pleased with the outcome of the vote. We look forward to working with our team to support our company’s continued recovery and meeting our customer commitments now and into the future.” – Ben Nimmergut, vice president and functional chief engineer for Production Engineering

articles.title_orig: $1.7 million raised in scheme for Hamas, including from U.S. donors, prosecutors say
articles.title_zh: $1.7 million raised in scheme for Hamas, including from U.S. donors, prosecutors say
articles.content_orig:
Nearly three years after Hamas' Oct. 7 attack on Israel, federal prosecutors allege that more than $1.7 million was funneled to the terrorist group Hamas, including hundreds of thousands of dollars from donors in the United States.
Saleem Alzaq, a 45-year-old Gaza man who prosecutors allege is a longtime Hamas member, was charged with helping operate the fundraising campaign claiming to provide humanitarian aid, according to an indictment unsealed Thursday.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq and his co-conspirators raised funds under the guise of providing food and winter necessities to Palestinians in Gaza between January 2020 and December 2025. The campaigns raised more than $1.7 million, including at least $626,000 from U.S.-based donors, according to the indictment.
Alzaq has been a Hamas member since at least 2017, prosecutors say, and has allegedly posted Hamas propaganda on social media, including posts celebrating the Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq operated an international fundraising campaign spanning the U.S. and France. Co-conspirators in France allegedly helped collect and transfer money, while two brothers from Louisiana allegedly contributed about $105,000 and a Florida man allegedly provided nearly $50,000 to the terror network.
Alzaq was charged with one count each of conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, conspiring to commit money laundering and conspiring to defraud the United States. The first three charges each carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if convicted, while the conspiracy to defraud charge carries a maximum of five years. He has not been arrested, and prosecutors say he's been in Gaza during the alleged crimes.
The indictment alleges Alzaq launched a new fundraising campaign on Oct. 7, 2023, that claimed to raise money for Gazans injured that day. The campaign remained open until about Oct. 12 that year, prosecutors said.
Investigators also conducted an undercover operation that prosecutors say provided evidence that Alzaq knew donations were reaching Hamas.
In November 2025, an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a New York-based Hamas supporter contacted Alzaq on Snapchat, according to prosecutors. Alzaq allegedly told the officer he had ways to receive money in New York and offered to connect the officer with contacts there.
The following month, Alzaq allegedly told the undercover officer that he worked with people like the officer who wanted to get money to "the Green," which prosecutors say was a reference to Hamas. He allegedly said he received money and gave it to "the Green," but that it would be difficult to provide proof because Hamas members avoided using identification.
Alzaq also allegedly told the undercover officer that he could deliver money monthly using coded language, including "bread," "bakeries," "buy bread" and "give it to the bakeries."
Prosecutors cited earlier Snapchat messages in which Alzaq allegedly discussed using similar language with a U.S.-based Hamas supporter. After the supporter asked him in January 2024 about money sent to "the bread people," Alzaq allegedly responded that he had "learned the way" and could deliver to them "whatever you want."
The indictment also alleges Alzaq advised donors not to reference Hamas to prevent their accounts from being shut down, including instructing followers in October 2024 not to write "Free Palestine" or "long live Hamas" on donations to his PayPal accounts.
"Our intelligence analysts uncovered this international finance network and built the case that exposed more than $2 million being funneled to Hamas," NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement. "Saleem Alzaq, a leader in Hamas' military arm responsible for planning and carrying out terrorist attacks, and the other defendants allegedly solicited donations under the guise of humanitarian aid and then directed that money to Hamas."

articles.title_orig: Hochul Names Letitia James as Special Prosecutor in Cornell Case
articles.title_zh: Hochul Names Letitia James as Special Prosecutor in Cornell Case
articles.content_orig:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor in investigating the alleged gang rape of a woman at Cornell University.
The woman has alleged she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house. The case, which stems back to 2024, was reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight.
"New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I've lost faith in the Tompkins County DA's ability to fairly oversee it," Hochul said.
The announcement means District Attorney Van Houten is no longer overseeing the case.
The BBC has contacted Van Houten's office for comment.
He has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold.
Van Houten reopened the case after the civil lawsuit and said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office.
"The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued," Hochul said in a statement.
James could prosecute any offences that might be found during her investigation and present evidence to a grand jury, Hochul said.
James, who is the state's chief legal officer, said on X that she stood ready "to lead a process guided by the facts and the law".
"The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly," James added.
Hochul and James are scheduled to provide an update on the investigation on Friday morning local time.
The woman at the centre of the case, identified anonymously as Jane Doe in court documents, filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September.
Jane Doe is a placeholder name sometimes used in US law for privacy or anonymity reasons.
She alleged that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven.
The case was initially referred to Van Houten, the top prosecutor in the county, in 2024.
Van Houten said his office did not bring charges at the time because he had only seen a statement from Doe implying the incident was consensual and that she had not been drugged.
This week, his office announced it would be reopening the case - less than two weeks after Doe filed her civil lawsuit.
Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.
Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, has accused the district attorney of repeatedly changing his story amid news coverage of the case.

articles.title_orig: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.title_zh: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.content_orig:
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in a critical condition in hospital after Tennessee authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer says.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution on Wednesday had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, raised a number of questions, including what went wrong? And what happens next?
A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who has halted executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year.
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder a year earlier of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
Pike was scheduled to be put to death in Tennessee on Wednesday evening local time. The injections were allowed by the Supreme Court at the 11th hour.
Pike was given two injections of the drug pentobarbital, but her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have not explained why the dosage given to Pike was non-fatal.
Opponents of the death penalty said it was difficult to know what went wrong, because part of Pike's execution happened behind a curtain.
Maya Foa, the head of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "Lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
The Tennessee correction department said Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility, while one of her lawyers said on Wednesday that she was being given "life-saving measures" in hospital.
On Thursday, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters: "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment."
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine, told the BBC in an email: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she [Pike] will have a brain injury."
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier.
A Supreme Court case from 1947 allowed the state of Louisiana to send Willie Francis, a teenager whose first execution attempt failed when he was 17 years old, back to the electric chair.
The court found a second execution would not violate the Constitution's prohibitions against double jeopardy or cruel and unusual punishment and Francis was executed aged 18.
"If the question is, is it likely the federal courts would intervene in a second attempt? I'm afraid the answer is a resounding no," Mills said of Pike's case.
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded".
But the department said in a statement the lethal injection chemical had "consistently been effective".
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Colleen Slemmer's killers met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
She was found with an inverted pentagram - a symbol associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest.
Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17.
Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
Colleen's mum, May Martinez, drove 11 hours from Florida to attend the execution, she told People , alongside with her husband Raul.
She said: "I wanted her [Pike] to remember who Colleen was and what they've done and never forget that thought, no matter where she goes."
Shipp was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole and he remains in prison.
He was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time.

articles.title_orig: Nike plans job cuts under sweeping restructuring plan
articles.title_zh: Nike plans job cuts under sweeping restructuring plan
articles.content_orig:
Nike on Thursday posted a mixed fiscal first quarter and announced a restructuring plan that will lead to layoffs starting next year.
The company also offered a full-year outlook, saying it expects revenues to decline by a high-single digit percentage in fiscal 2027. Nike also said it expects adjusted earnings per share to be in a range of $1.15 to $1.35.
Shares of Nike fell roughly 3% in extended trading Thursday.
Here's what the company reported for the period compared to what analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Nike reported net income of $712 million, down 2% from $727 million the year prior.
Revenue fell 4% to $11.21 billion. The retailer said Nike brand revenues took a hit largely due to sustained declines in the China business. Revenue in the market dropped 26%. CEO Elliott Hill said on a call with analysts that the company is "moving with urgency" to improve its business in the region.
Its North America revenue came in at $5.13 billion, just above estimates of $5.11 billion, according to StreetAccount. Nike also reported gross margin of 42.8% compared to estimates of 42.4%.
"Despite that progress, our Nike performance business is not yet large enough to offset the pressure we're seeing in Nike Sportswear, Jordan Brand, and Greater China," Hill told analysts. "We're taking deliberate actions to strengthen those businesses, but realizing the full benefit of those efforts will take time."
Nike's sportswear segment, which Hill said accounted for just under half of the quarter's revenue, fell by a low-double digit percentage.
" Overall, there's a lack of energy in the lifestyle space right now, which is impacting traffic," he said on the call. "Yes, the consumer is cautious, but as the leader in the industry, it's on us to bring more creativity to sportswear."
The sneaker giant also announced a restructuring plan to "position Nike for long-term growth." The strategy is expected to result in layoffs beginning in 2027, though the company did not provide any further details on how many jobs it would cut.
"This work will result in fewer roles across Nike, and I want to acknowledge that news like this creates uncertainty. I don't take that lightly," Hill wrote in a letter to the company.
The cuts are the third round of layoffs Nike has announced this year.
The company said it plans to focus on its supply chain modernization, organizing into three geographies, building a new campus in India and changing its work and workforce. Those geographic regions will be the Americas; the Asia Pacific and Greater China; and Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
The strategy, which Nike has dubbed Pace, is expected to deliver approximately $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031. It'll also result in a 15-cent restructuring expense to fiscal 2027 earnings per share, the company added.
"We expect Pace to streamline decision making, so we can capture demand faster and improve productivity, while also creating greater capacity to invest in what has always set Nike apart: serving athletes, creating industry-leading innovation and building the world's strongest sports brands," Hill said on the conference call.
The retailer has been in the midst of a turnaround plan, focused on improving separate parts of its business at different rates based on priority. The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions and higher inflation lead to slower spending.
Shares of Nike have plummeted more than 40% this year.

President Donald Trump announced U.S. troops will leave Iraq by the end of September, ending a 23-year presence.
The U.S. military has completed the withdrawal of American forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base in Iraq, ending its Operation Inherent Resolve mission, U.S. Central Command announced Wednesday.
The departure closes the Iraq chapter of the U.S.-led military mission launched against ISIS in 2014, while shifting primary responsibility for the country's security to Iraqi forces. The broader counter-ISIS campaign is not ending, however, with the U.S.-led task force relocating its headquarters to Jordan and operations continuing in Syria .
"Job well done to the tens of thousands of American service members, diplomats, and civilian personnel who answered the call in Iraq," CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.
US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM
Soldiers from the U.S.-led coalition forces are seen during the handover of the K1 Air Base to the Iraqi Army from the U.S.-led coalition in Kirkuk, Iraq on March 29, 2020. (The Associated Press)
"Because of your grit, sacrifice and professionalism, ISIS no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq’s national security and Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, now possess the capacity, leadership, and operational independence to unilaterally manage threats to their homeland," Cooper said.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called the departure the formal conclusion of Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq and said it marked a transition "from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship."
MOTORCYCLE PATROLS IRANIAN CITIES, CHECKPOINTS RISE AS REGIME BRACES FOR UNREST
The Pentagon said the U.S. will continue providing targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi forces even after the withdrawal, while Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga, take the lead in keeping ISIS remnants suppressed.
Erbil Air Base in northern Iraq served as the main operational hub for Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve and hosted most of the roughly 1,500 American and coalition forces supporting counter-ISIS operations , according to CENTCOM.
U.S. and coalition forces began leaving federal Iraq last October as Washington and Baghdad moved toward a bilateral defense relationship. The final removal of personnel and equipment from Erbil completed that transition on Sept. 30. The withdrawal followed an agreement reached between Washington and Baghdad under the Biden administration in 2024 and carried forward under the Trump administration.
Admiral Charles Bradford "Brad" Cooper II, commander of U.S. Central Command, speaks during a joint press conference at CENTCOM headquarters at MacDill Air Force Base in Tampa, Florida, on March 5, 2026. (Octavio Jones/AFP via Getty Images)
Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve remains active and is now headquartered in Jordan, according to CENTCOM. U.S. forces also continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria alongside coalition partners and the Syrian government.
SYRIA OFF US TERROR BLACKLIST AFTER NEARLY 50 YEARS AS TRUMP ADMIN CLEARS INVESTMENT HURDLE
The U.S. has roughly 4,000 troops stationed in Jordan, where American forces will continue monitoring the ISIS threat. Muwaffaq Salti Air Base hosts U.S. combat aircraft and has itself become a target during the conflict with Iran. Three U.S. service members were killed in an Iranian attack on the base in July.
"As we step back and hand full primary responsibility for Iraq’s security to the Government of Iraq and the brave people of Iraq, U.S. and coalition forces stationed across the region will remain ready to respond to any ISIS threats that arise," Cooper said.
"Maintaining our vigilance and readiness is essential to protecting the U.S. homeland and strengthening regional security," he added.
The withdrawal ends a U.S. military presence in Iraq that was reestablished in 2014, when Iraqi authorities sought international assistance as ISIS captured large areas of the country. U.S. troops had previously left Iraq in 2011 following the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein.
With U.S. forces leaving by Sept. 30 and as Baghdad tries to rein in Iran-backed militias, Iraq could also be entering its most dangerous period since ISIS seized Mosul in 2014. (REUTERS/Mohammed Ameen)
For the last several years, roughly 2,500 U.S. troops have been stationed in Iraq. The majority departed last year, leaving hundreds of troops in the northern Kurdish region until the final withdrawal.
The final departure comes as Iraq faces a separate security challenge from powerful Iran-backed militias operating inside the country. Baghdad has sought to bring weapons held by non-state groups under government control, but some of the most influential militias have resisted disarming.
IRANIAN PRESIDENT BLAMES US FOR MIDDLE EAST CONFLICT WHILE DENYING NUCLEAR AMBITIONS, OFFERS TO DILUTE URANIUM
The Pentagon explicitly identified those militias as one of the security challenges Baghdad will now be expected to confront.
"The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including ISIS remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq," Parnell said.
The withdrawal also reduces the number of U.S. military targets inside Iraq after American forces there faced repeated attacks by Iran-aligned groups following Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. During this year's war with Iran, seven of the 18 U.S. service members killed in Iranian attacks were killed in Iraq, according to Fox News reporting.
The withdrawal has drawn sharply different reactions inside Iraq. Iran-aligned groups celebrated the U.S. departure, while officials in the country's Kurdish region have raised concerns about the loss of American air-defense capabilities amid drone and missile threats.
Kurdish officials say their region has faced more than 1,000 Iranian drone and ballistic missile attacks since the war with Iran began Feb. 28, adding to concerns over the removal of U.S. forces and air-defense capabilities.
Thousands of ISIS fighters also remain in Iraq and Syria despite the collapse of the terror group's organized military threat. The Iraqi government has said its forces will continue operations against ISIS, while the Pentagon said the U.S. remains committed to preventing the group from reconstituting from Iraqi territory.

"The United States supports a strong sovereign Iraq that secures its borders, protects its people, and serves as the foundation for deeper commercial, diplomatic, and security cooperation between our two countries," Parnell said.

articles.title_orig: Alleged Hamas fundraiser to undercover agent: I have a network in New York
articles.title_zh: Alleged Hamas fundraiser to undercover agent: I have a network in New York
articles.content_orig:
Nearly three years after Hamas' Oct. 7 attack on Israel, federal prosecutors allege that more than $1.7 million was funneled to the terrorist group Hamas, including hundreds of thousands of dollars from donors in the United States.
Saleem Alzaq, a 45-year-old Gaza man who prosecutors allege is a longtime Hamas member, was charged with helping operate the fundraising campaign claiming to provide humanitarian aid, according to an indictment unsealed Thursday.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq and his co-conspirators raised funds under the guise of providing food and winter necessities to Palestinians in Gaza between January 2020 and December 2025. The campaigns raised more than $1.7 million, including at least $626,000 from U.S.-based donors, according to the indictment.
Alzaq has been a Hamas member since at least 2017, prosecutors say, and has allegedly posted Hamas propaganda on social media, including posts celebrating the Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Prosecutors allege Alzaq operated an international fundraising campaign spanning the U.S. and France. Co-conspirators in France allegedly helped collect and transfer money, while two brothers from Louisiana allegedly contributed about $105,000 and a Florida man allegedly provided nearly $50,000 to the terror network.
Alzaq was charged with one count each of conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, conspiring to commit money laundering and conspiring to defraud the United States. The first three charges each carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if convicted, while the conspiracy to defraud charge carries a maximum of five years. He has not been arrested, and prosecutors say he's been in Gaza during the alleged crimes.
The indictment alleges Alzaq launched a new fundraising campaign on Oct. 7, 2023, that claimed to raise money for Gazans injured that day. The campaign remained open until about Oct. 12 that year, prosecutors said.
Investigators also conducted an undercover operation that prosecutors say provided evidence that Alzaq knew donations were reaching Hamas.
In November 2025, an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a New York-based Hamas supporter contacted Alzaq on Snapchat, according to prosecutors. Alzaq allegedly told the officer he had ways to receive money in New York and offered to connect the officer with contacts there.
The following month, Alzaq allegedly told the undercover officer that he worked with people like the officer who wanted to get money to "the Green," which prosecutors say was a reference to Hamas. He allegedly said he received money and gave it to "the Green," but that it would be difficult to provide proof because Hamas members avoided using identification.
Alzaq also allegedly told the undercover officer that he could deliver money monthly using coded language, including "bread," "bakeries," "buy bread" and "give it to the bakeries."
Prosecutors cited earlier Snapchat messages in which Alzaq allegedly discussed using similar language with a U.S.-based Hamas supporter. After the supporter asked him in January 2024 about money sent to "the bread people," Alzaq allegedly responded that he had "learned the way" and could deliver to them "whatever you want."
The indictment also alleges Alzaq advised donors not to reference Hamas to prevent their accounts from being shut down, including instructing followers in October 2024 not to write "Free Palestine" or "long live Hamas" on donations to his PayPal accounts.
"Our intelligence analysts uncovered this international finance network and built the case that exposed more than $2 million being funneled to Hamas," NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement. "Saleem Alzaq, a leader in Hamas' military arm responsible for planning and carrying out terrorist attacks, and the other defendants allegedly solicited donations under the guise of humanitarian aid and then directed that money to Hamas."

articles.title_orig: Renée Good’s family sues Trump officials, saying death was ‘not an accident’
articles.title_zh: Renée Good’s family sues Trump officials, saying death was ‘not an accident’
articles.content_orig:
The partner of Renee Good, a Minneapolis woman who was fatally shot by an immigration officer in January , spoke publicly about her death for the first time Thursday as the family announced that they have filed two federal civil lawsuits.
“She was pure love, and she was funny, and she was smart, and she was gorgeous,” Becca Good said at a news conference, becoming emotional as she discussed attending back-to-school night and preparing to celebrate Halloween with their children alone.
“Every single one of these moments for all of her babies and for everyone up here was a monumental moment, and she should be here for all of them. We were all robbed,” she said.
Earlier in the news conference, attorneys for Renee Good’s family announced lawsuits alleging wrongful death and excessive force in her Jan. 7 death.
One lawsuit seeks to hold the United States liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act for the actions of federal agents. It alleges wrongful death, battery, assault, false imprisonment, emotional distress and negligence.
The second suit names Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot Good, as well as several federal officials, including White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.
“Every morning she’s my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama and how I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” Becca Good said.
Renee Good’s brother, Brent Ganger, said her death was “completely senseless.”
“We file these two lawsuits today to put officials on notice that we have not forgotten,” he said.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A representative for Ross could not immediately be identified.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the office will “vigorously defend” the claims in the lawsuits. Bis also shared a statement from President Donald Trump, who said Good’s “actions were pretty tough.”
“When you look at the way that car was pulled away ... there are a couple versions of that tape that are very very bad,” Trump said.
Good, 37, was fatally shot in the driver’s seat of her SUV during a Jan. 7 encounter with Ross. The killing occurred about a month after the Trump administration deployed 3,000 immigration agents to the Twin Cities in what officials have dubbed Operation Metro Surge. Agents descended on Minnesota after right-wing influencers drew attention to a state fraud scandal involving Somali nationals.
The operation triggered massive protests and significant pushback from state leaders. It ended in February .
The shooting was captured on cellphone video. It showed Good’s partner, Becca Good , standing outside the SUV calling Ross “big boy” and telling him to remove the covering from his face. Other officers at the scene could be heard telling Good to get out of the car. In the video, Good is seen turning the steering wheel away from Ross and beginning to drive.
Multiple gunshots can be heard in the video before Good’s SUV crashes into a parked car. In a separate video recorded by Ross, a male voice could be heard saying “f-----g b----” moments before the crash.
Trump administration figures, including President Donald Trump and Noem, defended Ross’ actions and claimed Good was an agitator who tried to run over the officer with her vehicle. Witnesses told NBC News at the time that Ross didn’t appear to be in the direct path of the SUV.
Noem said Ross was treated at a hospital for injuries he sustained in the incident and was released soon after. A DHS official previously told NBC News that Ross sustained internal bleeding but did not elaborate on his injuries.
Attorney Antonio M. Romanucci, who is representing Good’s family, said he hopes the lawsuits “are the beginning of the ultimate legal weapon in uncovering the truth behind this unlawful use of deadly force and the nefarious conspiracies behind the invasion of American cities by American law enforcement officers.”
Weeks after Good’s killing, Customs and Border Protection agents shot and killed Alex Pretti , a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, in Minneapolis.
Minyvonne Burke is a senior breaking news reporter for NBC News.
