articles.title_orig: Wichita founder flexes Startup World Cup win as his company swells into fitness industry
articles.title_zh: Wichita founder flexes Startup World Cup win as his company swells into fitness industry
articles.content_orig:
October 1, 2026  | Taylor Wilmore
Miguel Johns, founder of Milton AI, pitches his company during the Wichita regional Startup World Cup competition at the community's Launch Week; photo courtesy of the Kansas Department of Commerce
A nother Kansan is headed to San Francisco this fall for the Startup World Cup Grand Finale after winning Wichita’s regional pitch competition earlier this month. And founder Miguel Johns is wasting no time adding reps to his startup through an AI partnership with a Wichita gym.
Kansas-built Milton AI has teamed with Optimal Performance — adding the gym’s owners to Milton’s cap table as partners — as the company works to bring its technology into the facility.
“We partnered with them as a customer and as a partner in the company,” said Johns. “Since then, we’ve been working shoulder to shoulder, designing this thing and getting it ready for every independent gym in the world.”
The Optimal Performance deal gives Milton a working gym in which to develop and test its technology, while owners Bethany and Landon Langston bring two decades of experience running an independent fitness business to the product.
Milton is building toward a system that can handle billing, scheduling, coaching and other day-to-day operations that currently require multiple software products.
Finalists in the Wichita regional Startup World Cup competition: Craig Mason, Myndset; Robert Feeney, Knowledge as a Service Inc.; Toni Jones, The Bizy Shop; Bear Clark, EAR Micro/T10 Bespoke; and Miguel Johns, Milton AI; photo courtesy of the Kansas Department of Commerce
The relationship started with Johns — a Pipeline Entrepreneur and veteran of Wichita-based NXTUS programming — knocking on gym doors around his Kansas community. Milton had already spent years in development as an AI coaching product, but Johns wanted to better understand the headaches facing what he calls the “owner coach” — someone running a gym while also training clients.
“Nobody was home the day I went out and knocked on all the doors except for Bethany at Optimal Performance. She answered,” said Johns.
Bethany took a quick look at what Milton was building and agreed to a longer conversation. The Langstons walked the startup through the systems they were using to run the business and the gaps between them.
“‘Here’s our real problems. Here’s all of our workflows. We’re in this moment with AI. Can we pull this off? Can you take Milton to the next level and just be our one-stop-shop so we can cancel these other four subscriptions and save $2,000 a month?’” Johns recalled Bethany asking.
The conversation pushed Milton beyond the coaching software it had originally built and toward a broader role inside the gym.
Johns first tried to build an AI coach nearly a decade ago, long before ChatGPT. His early effort was built around IBM Watson and eventually wound down.
ChatGPT’s arrival in 2022 gave him another shot.
“I remember playing with it for the first time and just thinking, I’ve been waiting for this my whole life. This is what I needed,” said Johns.
Milton’s earliest iterations focused on health care and diabetes prevention, drawing on Johns’ background in exercise science, personal training and nutrition coaching. The company eventually moved into fitness, where Johns had firsthand experience with coaching and gym operations.
He spent about a year letting coaches and gyms use the Milton product while gathering feedback. The company began charging customers in 2025, and the feedback pointed toward a different opportunity: serving the gym owner responsible for the entire operation.
Billing, scheduling, customer management and coaching could all live in different systems, leaving owners to manage the technology while also spending much of their day training clients.
“Now we’re entering the space where we’ve started marketing ourselves as we’re the all-in-one solution, the all-in-one AI agent solution for gym owners,” said Johns.
Optimal Performance is among the first gyms where Milton is testing the full transition. The company is working through the practical side of moving customers from existing systems, including billing information, packages, credits and payment details.
Johns said Optimal Performance currently spends about $2,500 a month across five software products and could eventually pay about $500 a month for Milton.
Miguel Johns, founder of Milton AI, joins in a panel conversation during Wichita’s Launch Week; courtesy photo
Members use Milton to log workouts and meals, connect wearable data and stay engaged with their plans. The technology also handles administrative tasks such as scheduling and billing.
Johns sees another opportunity in giving trainers a clearer picture of a client’s health without requiring them to manually sort through every piece of information.
“Where Milton becomes spectacular is you can snap a photo of an InBody scan, a medical report, blood work, all these different things, and it’s picking up all these pieces from all your data and your insights and customizing what you should be doing specific to you,” said Johns.
The technology isn’t intended to replace the human relationship at the center of personal training.
“People want more human experiences, and a personal trainer can bring that human aspect to health,” said Johns.
Milton has recorded 150,000 engagements and 50,000 meals logged on the platform, according to Johns.
The partnership comes as Optimal Performance expands its own services. The gym is adding recovery rooms, a chiropractor and a physical therapist, with plans for additional health services. Milton is working alongside the Langstons as the facility expands and develops new workflows around those offerings.
“They are leading the design when it comes to those workflows and how it should operate in that regard,” said Johns.
Johns sees the changes at Optimal Performance as part of a broader evolution in fitness, where gyms could become a first stop for more preventive health services.
“We’ll just continue to help them turn what was just once a personal training gym into a true wellness hub where people go for their healthcare,” he said.
Working inside an operating gym is also giving Johns a closer look at what it takes to replace existing software without disrupting a business. The lessons will inform how the company approaches other independent gyms.
Miguel Johns smiles after being announced as the winner of the Wichita regional Startup World Cup competition; photo courtesy of the Kansas Department of Commerce
Milton’s work within Optimal Performance comes as the startup prepares for its next stage of growth.
Miguel Johns reacts after being named winner of the Wichita regional Startup World Cup competition; photo courtesy of the Kansas Department of Commerce

articles.title_orig: 'They’ll be hit very hard': Trump sends 9,000 troops to the Middle East after warning Iran strikes
articles.title_zh: 'They’ll be hit very hard': Trump sends 9,000 troops to the Middle East after warning Iran strikes
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. military is dispatching roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a U.S. official said Thursday. The bolstering of the American military presence comes as President Donald Trump warned anew that new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
The troop movement, which includes a third aircraft carrier, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump’s war against Iran as he ponders his next move, with midterm elections in the United States looming large and new signs that the nature of the conflict may be becoming more complex.
Trump has threatened that a post-midterm election escalation — despite his initial promises to Americans of a campaign that would last a matter of weeks — remains a viable option. Further complicating matters, Trump told reporters Thursday that early indications suggest that Iran is linked to the FlyDubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain and tried to crash an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday.
In an exchange with reporters at the White House, Trump raised the connection when asked by a reporter if there were any links between the pilot behind the attack and Tehran.
“I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is ‘yes,’ but we’re working on it right now,” Trump said, without offering details.
Trump added that if the link to Iran is established, the United States would retaliate. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in a Fox News interview earlier Thursday that investigators believe the FlyDubai suspect underwent “Islamist, radical indoctrination” but did not provide further details.
“Oh, they’ll be hit very hard, don’t worry,” Trump said. “You just ask them. They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”
Meanwhile, the group of ships now en route to the Middle East together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines.
It includes the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, which recently deployed with the cruiser USS Chosin, and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships.
It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October, according to the U.S. official, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the U.S. naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
The carriers USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington are in the region now, along with the USS Boxer amphibious readiness group. The Washington is typically deployed to the Pacific Ocean, but it was moved to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose arduous deployment resulted in the crew being at sea for more than 260 days straight.
Trump, in a Time magazine interview published Thursday, also raised the prospects of new strikes, saying it is “possible” that he will ramp up bombing in Iran after the Nov. 3 elections in the United States.
When pressed, Trump said he could not go into further detail about his strategy.
“I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?” Trump said.
He said in the interview, conducted Monday, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because “things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.”
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to “open up” the Strait of Hormuz, the key energy shipping corridor, but said the overall proposal was “not good enough.”
Asked if the increasingly unpopular war would threaten Republican Party chances in November, Trump at first responded, “It’s possible.” But then he added, “It should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”
The president said “100% of the people” oppose Iran having nuclear attack capabilities “including worldwide.”
“So, when you say it that way, it would help,” Trump added. “If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”
Yet, there’s also growing concern that Tehran might be turning to asymmetrical tactics following the FlyDubai attack and another suspicious incident in the U.K.
Authorities believe that Iran might be looking to shift strategy just as the U.S. finds greater success in loosening Iran’s grip over the Strait of Hormuz and getting Gulf allies’ oil to market, while a Navy blockade is shutting down Iran’s own oil exports.
British authorities announced on Thursday the arrest of a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran .
The arrest of the 27-year-old man in Central London came after U.K. authorities arrested five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, in the early hours of Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base
The base has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail .
Madhani reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Seung Min Kim and Will Weissert in Washington contributed to this report.

China’s major refiners have suspended most refined fuel exports for October as Beijing prioritizes domestic supply security, removing another source of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel from an already severely constrained global market.
PetroChina has cancelled several gasoline and jet fuel cargoes scheduled for October, while Zhejiang Petrochemical did not schedule exports during China’s week-long National Day holiday, Reuters reported, citing four people familiar with the matter. articles.title_orig: Trump’s Supreme Court grievance grows as new term looms
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Supreme Court grievance grows as new term looms
articles.content_orig:
Asked specifically what he wants from his Supreme Court nominees, the president replied, “I do like loyalty, yeah.”
Donald Trump’s tantrum in February after the Supreme Court rejected his tariffs policy was extreme , even by his standards. The president not only condemned the six-member majority as “a disgrace to our nation,” but he also insisted that the justices who dared to rule in a way he didn’t like were “very unpatriotic and disloyal to our Constitution.”
Asked then whether he regretted nominating Justices Amy Coney Barrett and Neil Gorsuch, Trump didn’t answer the question directly, though he said he considers their role in the ruling “an embarrassment to their families.”
In his latest Time magazine interview, the president was even more direct on the subject. From the article :
Yet with so much at stake — for the country and the world, for his party and his own power — Trump can seem curiously preoccupied. During a 75-minute Oval Office interview with TIME, he was discursive and grievance-fueled, veering from the crises of his presidency to resentments old and emerging. He said he regretted appointing Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court, after they ruled against him on tariffs, mail ballots, and birthright citizenship. “I gave them the position of a lifetime,” he said, “and they voted against me often.”
The transcript of the interview added remarkable details. Asked specifically if he regretted nominating Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett, Trump said he did — and then he kept going.
“The Democrats stick like glue — those three, they virtually never vary,” the president said, referring to Justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson. “You can come up with the worst thing in the world and they’ll vote as a group. And while I don’t like it, there’s something I admire about it: There’s loyalty. So they have loyalty to Barack Hussein Obama. They have loyalty to Biden, even though Biden doesn’t even know who the hell they are. He wouldn’t know. He doesn’t even know what the Supreme Court is.”
The petty and unhinged whining didn’t stop there. After an additional harangue about the birthright citizenship and tariff rulings — which really weren’t close calls, and which legal experts of every ideological stripe expected him to lose — Time asked, “You mentioned the word loyalty a moment ago. Is that what you want from your Supreme Court picks?”
The president replied, “I do like loyalty, yeah.”
To be sure, the rhetoric was not altogether surprising. As recently as April, Trump declared by way of his social media platform that “certain” conservative justices on the court have “gone weak, stupid, and bad.” A month later, on Mother’s Day, Trump broke new ground, publishing a 544-word screed in which he said Gorsuch and Barrett “have hurt our Country so badly!” He added, “[I]t’s really OK for them to be loyal to the person that appointed them.”
The problem with these rants isn’t just the impropriety or errors of fact and judgment. Collectively, what they also offer is a reminder that Trump still doesn’t understand how the government works in the United States.
As he sees it, if his administration does something illegal, then it’s incumbent on Supreme Court justices he appointed to simply look the other way — out of “loyalty.”
Indeed, Trump seems utterly baffled by the idea that he could appoint Supreme Court justices who, in turn, sometimes evaluates cases on the merits, which is, the last time I checked, their literal job. In other words, the president keeps publicly complaining not about justices being corrupt, but about justices not being corrupt enough to make him happy.
It’s tempting to think Trump would keep these attitudes private, perhaps limiting his complaints to close allies behind closed doors, but he instead keeps sharing them publicly, as if it were normal for a president to make these ridiculous complaints.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Bond Yields Hit Highest Level Since 2002
articles.title_zh: U.S. Bond Yields Hit Highest Level Since 2002
articles.content_orig:
The bond market is in an unrelenting sell-off. In the latest dubious milestone for US Treasuries, the yield on the 10-year benchmark note just hit its highest level since the dot-com bust.
American government bonds remain the world’s most important financial market, widely considered the safest place for investors to park their money. When times are tough, traders flee to the security of the US bond market.
That’s not what’s happening here. Just the opposite.
The reasons for the bond bust are numerous and, in some ways, counterintuitive: The US economy is strong – probably too strong, supported by massive AI spending . Inflation is too high, with prices pushed up by rising fuel costs. The Federal Reserve will probably try to slow all that down again.
The weak bond market and rising yields are hurting Americans’ borrowing power. Interest rates tied to the bond market, including mortgages and auto loans, continue to surge. The rate on a 30-year home loan topped 7% for the first time since early 2025 last week.
Meanwhile, investors keep heading for the bond market exits, selling off bonds and demanding higher rates at government bond auctions as inflation continues to rise. Higher prices degrade investments over time, and bondholders want to ensure they’re compensated for the effects of higher gas and diesel prices on their investments.
That’s sending yields ever higher, breaking through barriers not seen in decades. The 10-year yield on Thursday hit 5.34%, its highest level since 2002. The 30-year Treasury yield also hit a 24-year high, rising as high as 5.69%.
“There is carnage in the bond market,” said Neil Wilson, strategist at investment bank Saxo. “The worry is that US growth is way stronger than expected.”
Treasury yields pulled back on Thursday: The 10-year yield ended the day at 5.24%, still its highest level since 2007.
Analysts expect yields to remain elevated. US government data keeps showing evidence of a hot economy, maybe even an overheating economy.
A stronger-than-expected report on gross domestic product , the broadest measure of US economic activity, was released Wednesday, in addition to an inflation report that showed prices rising well above the Fed’s target. Some bondholders are sending yields higher in anticipation that the Fed will continue to raise its benchmark lending rate after increasing it last month for the first time since 2023 .
Why you should care about the bond market
Unemployment is low – the September jobs report on Friday is expected to show the unemployment rate remained at 4.1%, a level economists call “full employment.” Consumer spending remains robust, fueled by a strong stock market. And annual AI infrastructure spending is now measured in the trillions of dollars and is expected to keep growing – even as rates keep rising – over the course of the decade and beyond.
Debt concerns have also weighed on the bond market, as massive government spending from both political parties is putting the country on an unsustainable fiscal path.
The bond market’s problems are hardly isolated to the United States. Debt concerns and resurgent inflation as a result of high oil and fuel prices have sent rates higher all around the world. The 30-year UK government bond just hit 6% Thursday for the first time since 1998. The 10-year yield in France rose as high as 4.95% and hit its highest level since 2002.

articles.title_orig: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.title_zh: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.content_orig:
The family of Renee Good, from left; father Tim Ganger, mother Donna Ganger, brother Luke Ganger and brother Brent Ganger, listen during a news conference after the family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
The family of Renee Good , the 37-year-old killed last January by a federal agent during the Trump administration's immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed two civil lawsuits against the federal government Thursday.
One of the lawsuits, against the United States government itself, is essentially a wrongful death case, arguing that Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who killed Good, violated his agency's own policies and the Fourth Amendment by using excessive force.
It is seeking damages for Good's family for the suffering she experienced in the final moments of her life. And also for her partner, Becca Good, who witnessed the killing. The lawsuit says she has suffered intense emotional distress from what she has experienced. Ross shot Renee Good several times in her car. At the time, federal officials claimed she had weaponized her vehicle, though video evidence contradicted that.
The other lawsuit is rarer, alleging that federal officials engaged in a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of people in Minnesota.
It argues that Good's death was the "predictable and intended product" of the immigration crackdown in the state and that Ross' actions were in furtherance of a "carefully planned, coordinated effort" to make Somali and Hispanic people the "object of aggression and abduction" and to silence the people "who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign."
In making that argument, the lawyers, with the firm Romanucci & Blandin, relied on the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, which was used to combat the terrorism wrought by the KKK during the Reconstruction era.
"I would say the second lawsuit is very unusual," Rachel Moran, a law professor at the University of St. Thomas, told NPR. "It was immediately striking to me because the Trump administration has been aggressively using conspiracy charges , including here in Minnesota, against people involved in protesting the administration's immigration tactics."
Moran said the lawyers in the Good lawsuits seem to be "turning that tactic on its head" by arguing that administration officials are involved in an illegal conspiracy themselves.
According to Ben Berkman, one of the lawyers representing Good's family, the first lawsuit is about what federal officers did to Renee Good on a Minneapolis street last winter. The second is about why those officers were on that street in the first place.
"It reaches the agent who fired those shots at Renee and it reaches every official who put him on the street that day," Berkman said. "No mask, no badge and no title in the administration puts anyone above that law."
Those federal officials include Ross, but also White House adviser Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House Border czar Tom Homan, and former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, among others. NPR reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment, but did not hear back.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We intend to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits."
The lawsuit also lists 10 federal agents who were also present at the scene as John Does, noting that the federal government has not released their identities and that they were wearing masks at the time of the killing.
The civil charges also underscore a lack of criminal charges . DHS has provided little public indication that it is investigating Good's death or the death of Alex Pretti at the hands of Border Patrol agents a few weeks later in Minneapolis. According to The Trace, a news site that focuses on gun violence, nine people have been killed by immigration agents since President Trump took office again last year.
A memorial for Renee Good, who was killed by federal agents in Minneapolis in January, remains in place at the site of her death, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
At the state level in Minnesota, local officials have also not filed charges or released the findings of any investigation. In a statement, a spokesperson for Hennepin County, where Minneapolis is located, told NPR that state and local officials are reviewing the evidence and that they will "communicate transparently when a decision is reached."
At the press conference held Thursday, Good's family seemed frustrated at the inaction on all levels. Civil suits, like the ones filed by the family today, have the potential to hold entire institutions accountable rather than just individual actors.
"The fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Brent Ganger, Good's brother, said. "We will not wait any longer. The time is absolutely now for accountability, for the deep damage done by ICE and others. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."
Brent and his mother, Donna Ganger, also testified before Congress last week at a hearing about fatal shootings by federal immigration officers.
In her first public appearance since the killing, Becca Good, Renee Good's partner, also spoke. She focused her words on who Renee was to her, calling her kind and loving, but also on what she has lost. Renee Good had three children, and Becca is still raising their youngest, a 6-year-old.
"This past August, I got ready to put our son in first grade. I bought him new shoes and a backpack and notebooks, pencil case, the whole nine yards. I went to Back To School Night on my own," Becca Good said. "She never missed a single moment. And this Halloween, it's our son's absolute favorite holiday. I'll take him trick or treating, without her hand in mine."

Google says Gemini will give you audio cues to help line up your camera if you ask about something that’s not in the shot. However, Google cautions users not to rely on Guided Vision for things like “navigation, safe-travel guidance, or obstacle detection,” or as a replacement for a cane or mobility aid.

articles.title_orig: Of Note: A Future Marine Corps Commandant’s World War I Anniversary Letter
articles.title_zh: Of Note: A Future Marine Corps Commandant’s World War I Anniversary Letter
articles.content_orig:
A 2022 addition to the John Archer Lejeune Papers in the Library of Congress Manuscript Division consists entirely of his letters home to his wife Ellie Murdaugh Lejeune during World War I. At the time, the future Commandant of the United States Marine Corps was a major general commanding the Army’s 2 nd Division as part of the American Expeditionary Forces. While many of his letters home describe wartime events, they also show a softer side not often associated with a man commonly referred to as “the greatest Leatherneck of them all.”
Perhaps the most tender of these is an October 23, 1918, letter in which John celebrated their anniversary alone while reflecting on his happy home life. “This is the anniversary of our wedding day, 23 years have passed by since that wonderful day and each year has been happier than its predecessor.” The separation gnawed at him. He wrote to Ellie, “I wish with all my heart that I were home with you tonight, so we could look at the moon and the stars together and tell each other of our love.” The photos of his wife and daughters that John lined up on his mantle were a poor substitute for the real thing.
Despite his responsibilities, the day found John in a wistful, nostalgic mood. “I have thought of you darling all the day long and have pictured to myself over and over again just how beautiful you were in your wedding dress. I can never forget those fleeting moments during the ceremony when we took our vows to each other and to God.” When the Lejeunes married in a small ceremony in the parlor of Ellie’s family home in 1895, she had worn a white crepe dress for the occasion.
Even a wedding anniversary could not keep the war away, however. Interspersed with the sentimentality was an update on the war. “My most earnest prayer is that peace may soon return to the world and that we may then be reunited never more to part,” wrote John. “Victory must be near though the road to be trod is still a bloody one.” As he did in many of his letters, John kept Ellie updated on his duties as a military officer. Ellie, in turn, served as John’s sounding board while he was away, along with keeping the household running.
John and Ellie were finally reunited the next summer in 1919 upon the war’s end. As John hurried down the gangplank of the USS George Washington , Ellie and their three daughters met him on the dock at Hoboken, New Jersey, to welcome him home. John and Ellie Lejeune are buried together at Arlington National Cemetery, never more to be parted.

Two years after a woman alleged a gang rape at Cornell University, renewed attention to the case and the limited consequences faced by the alleged perpetrators has raised questions about what higher education owes students who experience sexual assault on campus as well as how consent and intoxication are understood under New York law.
A woman identified as Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging that she was sexually assaulted, gang-raped, and pressured to take drugs and drink alcohol by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of Oct. 19, 2024. The lawsuit is filed against the fraternity, Doe’s sorority chapter, and Cornell University; it names Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris, and Scott Kretzschmar as defendants. Prosecutors said this week they were reopening a criminal investigation into the case after declining to press charges originally.
Separate attorneys for Kretzschmar and Lopes denied the allegations in statements to ABC , while Norris, via an attorney, denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use but acknowledged that he sent a message included in the complaint.
When sexual assault allegations of this kind occur on campus, they can be addressed in three distinct ways: through school disciplinary proceedings, criminal proceedings, and civil lawsuits.
Doe’s civil lawsuit alleges that Cornell failed to protect her. Her attorney has separately criticized authorities’ handling of the criminal investigation, although observers say what’s known as the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in state law could limit what prosecutors are able to charge.
Here’s what to know about how the case was handled—by Cornell and the criminal justice system—before, and what could happen next.
Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police in November 2024. According to her complaint, Cornell began its Title IX investigation on Jan. 14, 2025.
Title IX is a law dating back to 1972 that is meant to, among other things, ensure that a college investigates when there is sexual assault on campus. Central to this premise is that Title IX is meant to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
Read More: Trump’s Title IX Announcement Is Cruel. But It Does Not Change the Law
Doe’s attorney has said that Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students. Cornell has confirmed that its disciplinary process resulted in expulsions and suspensions, but has not disclosed individual outcomes. The lawsuit alleges negligence, breach of contract, and violations of New York law.
Cornell responded in a statement last week, saying that it could not confirm the individual disciplinary outcomes due to student privacy laws. However, the university clarified on Monday that “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.”
“We take sexual violence extremely seriously,” the Sept. 21 statement said. “The Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault was launched shortly after this incident and issued a REPORT in March 2026.”
In a statement Monday, Kyle Kimball, Cornell’s vice president for university relations, said Chi Phi’s Cornell chapter closed in 2024 and the fraternity remains barred from campus.
But women’s rights advocates believe that the school might not have fulfilled its legal obligations in investigating the incident and taking appropriate actions toward those involved.
Title IX is a federal civil rights law meant to prohibit sex-based discrimination in any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.
Since Title IX was introduced, courts have found that the law requires institutions to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
“The reason why Title IX addresses sexual harassment, including sexual assault, is because of the very real impact that has on students’ ability to access education,” Shiwali Patel, a Title IX expert with the National Women’s Law Center, tells TIME.
According to the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), students who experience sexual assault are more likely to earn lower GPAs in school and are more likely to drop out of school altogether.
Patel points to Doe’s attorney’s account of her efforts to leave Cornell after the alleged assault. In a Sept. 28 interview with CNN, Thomas Giuffra—Jane Doe’s lawyer—said Cornell refused her family’s tuition-refund request, leaving her to spend another semester on campus.
“She was trying to leave the institution; she didn’t want to be there,” Patel says.
Cornell told People that it works with students seeking to take leave or withdraw and “regularly refunds payments if students are no longer enrolled.”
Giuffra also told CNN that Doe is no longer in college as of 2026.
Universities also have obligations to offer support regardless of a formal complaint or a finding of culpability. These can include counseling, academic adjustments, and housing or schedule changes. Patel says it remains unclear whether Cornell fully complied with its Title IX obligations because the supportive measures it provided Doe are not publicly known.
Regardless, the situation raises questions about what more schools can do for students, Patel says, providing some examples of the types of questions that a university might ask in the aftermath of this kind of incident: “Does she need extensions on exams? Does she need some time off, some leave? Does she need a housing shift if the fraternity house and her sorority house are close together? Does she need counseling? Did they provide a stay away order? What kind of support were they giving her to make sure she wouldn’t have to be retriggered and traumatized by running into them?”
Title IX also requires schools to investigate allegations through a reliable, impartial process—independently of criminal court systems, and using a lower burden of proof to determine if a student violated campus policy.
Cornell University publicly disclosed that it was investigating the allegation on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe went to the police, according to the lawsuit. The university sent an alert to students regarding a report of sexual assault and coercion into taking drugs at a fraternity house. The same day, Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity.
In response to an inquiry from TIME, Cornell said that its “Office of Civil Rights and the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards investigated the allegations against the individuals and the fraternity consistent with university policies and Title IX.”
“The university’s Title IX investigation was conducted over several months and included hearings where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days,” the university’s statement continued. “The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence in the university’s investigation.”
Cornell’s handling of the case unfolded amid shifting federal rules on campus sexual misconduct. A court vacated the Biden Administration’s Title IX rule on Jan. 9, 2025—five days before Cornell began its formal investigation, according to Doe’s complaint. The university held hearings that May, making the rules it applied a key question in assessing its response.
The Biden Administration had expanded Title IX regulations in April 2024—taking effect in August 2024—broadening the definition of sexual harassment and extending federal protections.

articles.title_orig: Tyler Erb Reflects on ‘Exponential’ Growth in First Year Back With World of Outlaws
articles.title_zh: Tyler Erb Reflects on ‘Exponential’ Growth in First Year Back With World of Outlaws
articles.content_orig:
October 1, 2026 at 3:27 pm
For the first time in a long time, Tyler Erb is approaching the end of a full-time national tour run in a positive frame of mind.
The New Waverly, TX native spent three years with the World of Outlaws Late Model Series presented by DIRTVision from 2016 through 2018, before shifting to the Lucas Oil Late Model Dirt Series from 2019 until 2023. Erb amassed 21 wins between them and a best points finish of fourth in 2019, but three years ago, he knew it was time for a change.
The next two seasons in 2024 and 2025 were what Erb affectionately called the “Fun Tour” – racing wherever he wanted, whenever he wanted. His travels produced 33 wins over two years, plus the 2024 DIRTcar Summer Nationals championship.
“Last time I ran a national tour, I was just mad at the world,” Erb said. “I had done it for, I don’t know, six, seven years actually. I was burned out because I didn’t feel like I got to go to some of the places I wanted to go. I didn’t get to race a whole year the way I thought I wanted to race, and that’s just do whatever I want to do, pick and choose. Not skip races, but just go to the ones that I feel like I had a really good chance to win. I got to do that for two years and was successful doing it.
“So, then I was like, ‘OK, I feel like I’ve done really good at picking and choosing and doing all that.’ So, I can check that off my list of stuff, self-goals that I have that no one cares about except me. And the next one I have would be to try to win an Outlaws championship. And in order to do that, you’ve got to do it and compete.”
That’s precisely what Erb and his Best Performance Motorsports team set out to do in their return to full-time World of Outlaws racing in 2026. Erb’s refreshed mindset and renewed sense of confidence has resulted in what could be described as the best year of his career. With five races remaining in the season, Erb sits in a career-high third in the championship standings, trailing only the two hottest Late Model drivers in America in Bobby Pierce and Nick Hoffman .
“I had kind of set my own goals, and being third in points is kind of within that range,” Erb said. “Winning four races is a little light on, you know, how many I was trying to win this year. But we still have five left or whatever, so there’s definitely a chance to make up for a lot of it. I would give it a B+, A-. Because Nick and Bobby are obviously really, really good. To be right there behind them and beat them on the nights we beat them, I feel like that’s good.”
It’s often said that you’re only as good as the competition you race against, and Erb credits his own progression this year to battling the same elite cast of characters night after night. It has made his own spot in the pecking order plain to see, as well as the areas that need to improve to take the next step into championship contention next season.
“Like right now, Nick and Bobby are ranked first and second in the [DirtonDirt] poll,” Erb said. “If you beat them however many times, you’re like, ‘OK, well, I beat them last week, so I can beat them this week.’ Where if you come in and you don’t beat them, and then you watch for a month and they run second, second, second and you win, you’re like, ‘Oh, I’ll beat them guys no problem.’ When you race them every night, you kind of realize their strengths and weaknesses and get an idea of how to beat them. It’s been good. You race some of the best competition night in, night out, it just makes you better.
“Going racing at different places and the stuff I did before definitely helps too, because you just race at all sorts of different racetracks and series and rules, you have to be able to adapt quick. But doing what we’re doing now, I think in the long run, the growth I’ve had this year is probably exponential compared to what I did the two years before. But I needed the two years of racing the ‘Fun Tour’ per se to grow in that aspect.”
Erb has never been afraid of doing things his own way both on and off the track. His car choice is one example, as Erb is one of only two World of Outlaws full-timers flying the flag for Rocket Chassis. That has created a bond between Erb and 2022 World of Outlaws champion Dennis Erb Jr. that goes back several years, and being in the same pit area every night has only strengthened the relationship.
“Dennis is an older me,” Erb said. “He’s done it, he’s kind of hard-headed, kind of his own person and there’s nothing wrong with that. I mean, for both of our sakes, if we won every race and it was the Dennis and Tyler show, that would be cool. It’s good to have somebody that you can lean on at times, and I feel like I do that for Dennis and Dennis does that for me with anything. His approach to a race and my approach, everybody’s a little bit different in a sense, but it is nice that I’m not the only lone ranger out there.
“I have Dennis, and then when Mark [Richards] or Josh Rice or whoever shows up, we all want to do good. We’re outnumbered to an extent right now, but I don’t look at it that way; I could care less. I know what I’m comfortable in and what I drive, and I think everybody in a Rocket has that same mindset. We’ve been in them for so long, it’s just what we’re comfortable with. We can make it work because we win races; we’ve just got to do it on a more consistent level.”
As Erb prepares to close the book on 2026 and look ahead to next season, he’s doing so at a point in life many dream of. His race team is on the rise and running up front more than ever, and away from the track, he’s about to become a first-time father with fiancée Emma Hodge. But is the rambunctious, short-fused Erb of old finally growing up? He’s not so sure.
“Nobody grows up, that’s such bulls**t,” Erb said. “I just know what I want to do, I’m very focused on it and have figured out how to balance it a little bit. Obviously, I’m getting married, having a kid, so that’s super exciting. I didn’t have any of that three years ago. I didn’t even know if I wanted that; I didn’t have an idea about it. Now, I’m very sure of what I want to do and get done, so it’s just a different mindset. Time goes on and opens your eyes to a lot of things.”
Erb will wrap up his season with the World of Outlaws Late Model Series presented by DIRTVision in the Modoc 100 at Modoc Speedway (Friday-Saturday, Oct. 23-24), followed by the Dave Smith Motors World of Outlaws World Finals at The Dirt Track at Charlotte (Wednesday-Saturday, Nov. 4-7). articles.content_orig:
Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei will be the first titles to use the new Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) library.
Since the launch of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) on PS5 Pro , players and developers have asked whether similar image-quality improvements could be brought to the PS5 console. PSSR analyzes game images pixel by pixel and uses AI to upscale them with more detail and stability than conventional approaches; until now, its computational demands made bringing that experience to PS5 impossible.
Today, we’re excited to announce Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR): a new performance tier of AI upscaling. Born from Project Amethyst, our AI graphics collaboration with AMD, this quick new evolution of PSSR is built on two key innovations:
With these, we are bringing the benefits of AI-guided upscaling to PS5. While PSSR remains the gold standard on PS5 Pro, QSSR provides some notable improvements to both image detail and image stability on PS5.
The first titles to use this innovative new library are Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei. Both are being patched today to offer QSSR as an additional graphics option on PS5.
Here’s what Insomniac Games and Sucker Punch Productions have to share about the benefits of this new technology:
“Our team at Insomniac works hard to make sure each of our games is a showcase of PlayStation hardware, and we’re excited for Marvel’s Wolverine to be one of the first titles to bring this new QSSR technology to players.
QSSR adds more pixel-level clarity and stability to our environments, bringing out extra detail amidst the busy streets of Madripoor, the dense alleyways of Shinjuku, and many other areas across Logan’s epic journey. It’s a perfect companion to the launch of Marvel’s Wolverine, and it brings a great taste of the PS5 Pro experience to our players on PS5.
Personally, I love seeing how the PlayStation tech teams continually improve the PS5 platform, and I’m excited for more games to make use of QSSR in the future!”
– Mike Fitzgerald, Head of Technology / Insomniac Games
“At Sucker Punch, we’re excited to bring QSSR to Ghost of Yōtei players so that they can experience the world we’ve created with even more clarity and detail. QSSR excels at resolving the fine details in our characters and environments and does so with a level of temporal stability that hasn’t been possible on the PS5 console until now. We’ve long wished that all PS5 players could experience the incredible image quality that PSSR brings to PS5 Pro, and QSSR is a positive step towards that goal!”
– Jasmin Patry, Lead Rendering Engineer / Sucker Punch Productions
QSSR will be offered broadly to all PlayStation developers, and we look forward to seeing these improvements in many more titles going forward!

'Outnumbered' co-host Kayleigh McEnany shares the story of Freddy, a now-famous German soccer fan whose U.S. trip continues for three weeks after his team's World Cup elimination.
Everyone remembers Freddy, right?
The World Cup guest from Germany stole the hearts of soccer fans all across America for his love of the host country, documenting his trip through the United States on social media and giving glowing reviews along the way.
German soccer fan Freddy's summer to remember concludes with a visit to the White House on Tuesday. In June, Freddy and his friends had the pleasure of meeting country star Ella Langley after a show in Oklahoma City. (FreddyLA7 / Getty Images)
Well, Freddy is back in the Lower 48, this time spending his days in the American South and enjoying the actual greatest sport on earth: college football.
THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!
The Fredster has been to Auburn and LSU to see a couple of SEC games, and this week he finds himself in the Magnolia State en route to Alabama for an Oktoberfest event over the weekend.
And what do you do when you find yourself in Mississippi for a couple of days? Go hang out in Jackson, of course!
Jackson, MS skyline including the State Capitol Building (iStock)
Wait, that can't be right. What, was Memphis already booked up for the week?
Yes, our dear Freddy has decided to make a stop in the capital city for a little RnR, and made the cardinal sin of thinking he was going for a stroll in gay old Paree instead of the deadliest city, per capita, in the contiguous U.S.
"Hey guys, Freddy here! Just thinking about maybe hitting up Buffalo Wild Wings for a quick bite to eat then walking through a literal warzone to take in the sights and sounds of the place."
Did this guy read the travel itinerary or what?
FIFA EYES WORLD CUP FORMAT EXPANSION FROM 48 TO 64 TEAMS: SHOULD THE US BE THE PERMANENT HOST?
This isn't the first time Freddy made a classic tourist mistake, as he has a well-documented ride on the MARTA in Atlanta from his days as a World Cup visitor.
The best part is that pretty much everyone on social media was trying to warn our lieber freunde about the dangers of Jackson, Mississippi.
While his followers were whipped up into a frenzy wondering if their dude from Deutschland was okay, Freddy apparently enjoyed a nice meal at the great American eatery known as Chili's and then returned safely to his hotel bed.
Chili's retro "Margarita Bar" celebrates one of the chain's signature drinks. (Chili's)
Maybe Freddy can try the lottery or head to Las Vegas next, since he likes playing the odds so much.
I don't know if it's ignorance or testicular fortitude, but our guy spent a night on the streets of Jackson and lived to tell about it.

articles.title_orig: 8 in 10 Americans disapprove of Trump on inflation. That’s extremely rare for a president
articles.title_zh: 8 in 10 Americans disapprove of Trump on inflation. That’s extremely rare for a president
articles.content_orig:
We don’t yet know how the 2026 midterm elections will shake out.
What we can say right now is that President Donald Trump’s handling of inflation is a historic liability — the likes of which we’ve rarely seen in modern American politics.
As many as 8 in 10 Americans now disapprove of Trump on that issue. That’s more than disapproved of presidents for wars gone wrong, botched crisis responses and even major scandals like Watergate.
A new AP-NORC poll on Thursday was the latest ugly data point for Trump. It showed Americans disapproved of him on cost-of-living issues by a stunning margin: 82% to 17%.
It’s rare to get even 70% of Americans to agree on anything political. But Trump has managed to unite 8 in 10 Americans against his handling of one of the country’s most important issues.
And this poll isn’t just some outlier. Here’s a brief recap of recent polls on this issue:
The level of disapproval on such a major issue has few precedents, though George W. Bush did face a 77% disapproval rating in a CBS News/New York Times poll for his handling of the economy near the end of his term after the 2008 financial crisis. In 1980, the same pollster showed Jimmy Carter’s disapproval on that issue peaking at 74% amid high unemployment and inflation.
One of the likeliest culprits for such high disapproval numbers would seem to be war. And those have been very unpopular. But not as unpopular as Trump’s handling of the cost of living. George W. Bush’s disapproval rating on the Iraq war peaked around 70% . Disapproval of Joe Biden’s withdrawal from Afghanistan peaked around two-thirds . And the Vietnam war led Lyndon Johnson to scrap his reelection bid in 1968, but his disapproval rating on the issue was only in the 60s .
In fact, the highest disapproval rating for a war appears to be Trump’s latest numbers on the Iran war. The CNN poll showed 73% disapproved of his handling of that.
When it comes to crises, as many as 64% disapproved of Bush’s handling of Hurricane Katrina, and Carter’s disapproval amid the Iran hostage crisis climbed into the mid-50s. Even Trump’s handling of the January 6 attack on the Capitol ( 67% in CNN polling ) wasn’t as lopsided as Trump and inflation right now.
As far as scandals, Ronald Reagan’s disapproval on the Iran-Contra affair reached as high as 69% in a January 1987 Washington Post-ABC News poll. And at the height of Watergate, as many as 71% of Americans disapproved of Richard Nixon on domestic issues. (We don’t have good approval polling from back then on Watergate, specifically.)
Speaking of Nixon, pardons have also tested Americans’ tolerance. But even Gerald Ford’s pardon of Nixon — which was supposed to have crippled Ford politically — only saw a disapproval rating in the 50s , according to polls compiled by the Roper Center for Public Opinion Research.
Indeed, about the closest Trump got previously to 80% disapproval on a major issue was another controversial set of pardons: his pardons of violent January 6 defendants last year. A Pew Research Center poll showed 74% of Americans disapproved of that.
You might be noticing a trend here. Many of the issues with the highest presidential disapproval ratings involve the same president: Trump. That includes the Iran war, the January 6 Capitol attack and the related pardons. But the disapproval he faces on inflation surpasses all of those issues.
You could perhaps understand why Republicans are suddenly anxious to pass legislation on affordability before the election.
Trump in a new Time magazine interview published Thursday said Americans shouldn’t hold him responsible for their affordability problems and again blamed inflation on Biden. (This despite inflation being higher today than it was when Trump took over last year.)
But the AP-NORC poll is the latest to suggest that strategy won’t work. It shows 65% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies for high prices more so than factors beyond his control. That number for Biden just before the 2022 midterm elections was much lower: 44% .
Perhaps Trump’s party can still do OK in the upcoming midterms. But if it does, it will be despite historic dissatisfaction with the president on voters’ clear No. 1 issue.

articles.title_zh: World ski body eyes financial reset after overspending and wants to add new events - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Skiing’s governing body was on track to spend all its cash reserves by 2028 and has now cut jobs while aiming to add new competitions to restore finances
GENEVA -- Skiing’s governing body was on track to spend all its cash reserves by 2028 and has now cut jobs while aiming to add new events to help restore finances.
The International Ski and Snowboard Federation’s rescue plan — steering away from expected annual losses of 20 million Swiss francs ($24 million) — was detailed at meetings this week ahead of the first winter season since new president Alexander Ospelt from Liechtenstein was elected by a single vote.
Rising concerns about spending during the five-year presidency of Johan Eliasch , the billionaire boss of the Head ski and sportswear brand, seemed to be decisive in the June election.
“We are in a serious situation, not a desperate one,” the ski body’s interim secretary general Urs Lehmann said in an interview on the sidelines of the week-long gathering in Geneva. “The FIS family deserved to have clarity where we are.”
An FIS office in Munich, Germany was closed and race prize money subsidies that began during the COVID-19 pandemic have been curbed. It's part of the financial reset for the governing body that oversees Alpine and cross-country skiing, freestyle and snowboarding, ski jumping and Nordic combined.
The World Cup race earnings leaders across the FIS disciplines last winter were the superstars of Alpine skiing who also won their overall titles.
Switzerland's Marco Odermatt won 741,000 euros ($832,000) in prize money from race organizers and Mikaela Shiffrin topped the women's list with 615,000 euros ($690,000) earned. Yet they were the only Alpine skiers to earn more than 400,000 euros ($450,000) from races across the five-month season.
Those totals also were boosted by FIS money that started during the pandemic and is no longer viable.
“If you add something, that’s easy," Lehmann, the 1993 men’s downhill world champion for Switzerland, told The Associated Press. “Taking it away again is super difficult and nobody did it over the last three years.”
Maintaining and increasing athlete prize money likely will mean more races spread around more venues that want to either join or be a more regular stop on the World Cup circuits.
“There is only one way — add competitions," Lehmann said. “Can we do this? Yes, because I’m a strong believer that our calendar has more space. We have more interested parties than we have spots today.”
Extra world championships are set to be added in the current down year of a four-year Olympic cycle which includes two editions of worlds.
Member federations were told at a specially convened FIS Summit in Geneva that “FIS is solvent today but in a critical point," according to a presentation.
Equity reserves had almost halved at the end of last year to about 43 million Swiss francs ($52 million) since 2021 when Eliasch was elected, after a second pandemic-hit season.
Total revenue for the four-year cycle through 2029 is set to double to almost 650 million Swiss francs ($783 million) yet expenses are rising at a faster rate.
Reserves are set to be exhausted by the end of the 2028 winter season, with reasons cited including a decline in the value of world championships broadcasting rights and rising broadcast production costs.
FIS members were told their governing body had been paying them too much while its staffing almost doubled from 50 to 98.
“We had to let go a bunch of our teammates unfortunately to become leaner, more efficient and also cost efficient,” said Lehmann, who joined FIS in a newly created chief executive role last year then resigned days before the presidential election.
“We have a plan but this plan works only if the FIS family is really standing together,” Lehmann said.
Long-term broadcast and commercial contracts mean the situation cannot change fast enough.
“In media rights, basically the deals are done until 2030. The effect of having a higher value we will only see in almost four years,” Lehmann said. "I am convinced that we are going to make it but everybody has to know where we stand today.”

articles.title_orig: School protests spread as fires, blockades deepen unrest in France
articles.title_zh: School protests spread as fires, blockades deepen unrest in France
articles.content_orig:
French students have set fire to bins and erected blockades outside schools in several cities, protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.
Several school principals were injured, harassed or assaulted during blockades at high schools on Thursday, according to reports from regional education authorities, prefectures and union representatives.
Police have already detained hundreds of protesters at the lycees, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France.
At Marseille’s Victor Hugo high school, the teachers were inadvertently splashed as a student attempted to throw petrol into a rubbish bin, local authorities said. Earlier, the prosecutor’s office had ⁠said the teachers had been assaulted and “doused in petrol”.
At another school in the city, Saint-Exupery high school, hundreds of young people surrounded a firetruck that had arrived to put out a blaze in the morning, police said. The attackers forced the firefighters to flee the vehicle, then set it alight.
In Nantes, firefighters extinguished a fire at a high school entrance following what regional education officials called a gathering “marked by violence towards staff”. In Strasbourg, trams were halted to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, and students burned barriers on tram tracks, authorities said.
“There are 35 of us per classroom. With 35 degrees Celsius [95 degrees Fahrenheit] in summer, it’s unbearable. There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms,” Raphael, a 17-year-old who withheld his surname for fear of reprisals, told the AFP news agency outside a protest in Strasbourg.
“The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors.”
His frustration echoes a wave of student anger that has spread across France since last week, as high school pupils protest and grievances snowball into nationwide unrest.
Some 340 demonstrations were under way outside high schools by mid-morning on Thursday, with more than 160 schools shut down as a result, police said.
University students joined in, blocking access to about 30 campuses, including in Paris and Marseille, according to a student union.
Authorities have reported many dozens of injuries – some from thrown objects, others reportedly from police riot-control projectiles.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police have opened internal investigations into brutality allegations involving three students.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu convened a crisis meeting and asked ministers to cancel upcoming official travel so authorities could focus on the demonstrations, his office said.
French Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that he would successively meet representative staff unions and parent and student associations on Friday.
The unrest has become entangled in the race to succeed President Emmanuel Macron next May. The government has accused the far-left France Unbowed party of encouraging the protests. Presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said Wednesday that his party “called for nonviolent methods of struggle” and criticised the government’s response as repressive.

articles.title_orig: World in Brief: Bond sell-off gathers speed; pilot stabbed on Israel-bound flight
articles.title_zh: World in Brief: Bond sell-off gathers speed; pilot stabbed on Israel-bound flight
articles.content_orig:
The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"
The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar.
Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia.
The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tabuk, a city in north-western Saudi Arabia.
The Indian embassy in the United Arab Emirates said Machchhar was "in good health and recovering well". Ambassador Deepak Mittal said he was "proud of Capt Smit for his bravery" and "very reassured" to meet him.
Netanyahu wrote on X that Machchhar "saved the lives of 174 people" and prevented "a catastrophic mid-air disaster".
Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later.
He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022 as an experienced pilot.
Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, told the BBC he remembered Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis.
"We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker."
Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.
His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".
An old friend who worked with him at SpiceJet, Capt Dharav Gosalia, described him as outgoing and "very jovial" .
Machchhar - whose nickname was "Smit Mac" - was a "disciplined flier" who had undergone years of training, he said, including from former Indian Air Force pilots who had moved into commercial aviation.
Gosalia (left) and Machchhar (right) have known each other since they were 20
Last year, Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.
Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work for his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]", he added.
Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.
"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.
He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.
"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.
At the time of the conversation, Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had needed to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues that had caused delays.
He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."
Indian social media has been awash with praise for Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.
What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel
Machchhar joined Flydubai in 2022
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.
The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.
Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.
At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.
But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.
He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.
The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Machchhar.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured.
"His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.
Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".
US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack.
"Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

articles.title_orig: A rosary in the Vatican for ‘peace for all the children in the world'
articles.title_zh: A rosary in the Vatican for ‘peace for all the children in the world'
articles.content_orig:
While one million children around the world offered up the Rosary for peace, about 1,300 of those voices were coming from the Vatican Gardens on the first day of the month dedicated to the RosaryâOctober 1. Children from parishes and schools around Rome gathered at the Grotto of Lourdes with Pope Leo XIV to kick off the Aid to the Church in Need initiative âOne Million Children Praying the Rosaryâ.
Representing the global dimension of this initiative, each of the five decades was recited in a different language: Italian, Spanish, Urdu, German, and Arabic.
This rosary starts a weeklong initiative drawing attention to âthe wounds and hopes of peoplesâ globallyâthe children of Ukraine and all the victims of war; families in Lebanon, Syria, and the Holy Land; persecuted Christians in Pakistan and around the world; reconciliation in South Sudan; and families in Cuba and Venezuela.
Before reciting the Marian prayer, Cardinal Kurt Koch, Prefect of the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, explained that this initiative is an invitation for children to discover that âtogether with Mary, they can bring the sufferings of the world to Jesus.â
âIt is precisely the voices of the youngest, who entrust themselves to him with confidence, that find a special welcome in the heart of God,â he stressed. Throughout the weekâOctober 1-7âcommunities around the world, separated by language and distance, will be united in their prayer for peace.
âAs we contemplate the risen Christ, we ask that fear and hatred may not have the final word,â Cardinal Koch said.
In his message, Pope Leo XIV stressed the importance of this initiative and his joy at being present with the children, parents, and priests.
Encouraging the children, the Pope reminded them that they are asking Jesus and Mary for âa special gift: peace for all the children of the world, especially those who live in places where there is war, in so many countries around the world.â
He described the rosary as a âsimple prayer that everyone can prayâ and called the flowers the children had offered at the beginning of each decade as a sign of love.
The Pope urged them to think about Jesus at the important moments of his life, âwhen he brought light and peace to many people.â These included Jesusâ baptism in the Jordan, turning water in wine at the wedding of Cana, proclaiming the Kingdom of God, his Transfiguration, and when he instituted the Eucharist in the Upper Room.
Pope Leo urged the children never to forget and be thankful for these moments when Jesus âgave us wonderful giftsâ and to âask him with confidence, all united: Give us peaceâ.
Concluding his message to the children and families, the Pope highlighted how those present in the Vatican Gardens throughout this week (October 1-7) are not the only ones praying. About one million voices are joining them in this prayer.
âThink about itâ, Pope Leo stressed: âFifty million âHail Marysâ rising to Heaven from every part of the world and in every language, asking for peace, joining together like one enormous Rosary, embracing all the continents, peoples, and nations of the world.â
By praying the rosary together at the Grotto of Lourdes, he reminded everyone present that they are committing themselves to behaving well wherever they are: at home, school, in catechism class, with their parents, and when they play.
âPrayers must also be accompanied by good deeds and acts of love,â Pope Leo explained. âThat is how peace grows.â

articles.title_orig: Sony announces QSSR AI upscaling tech for base PS5 in Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei
articles.title_zh: Sony announces QSSR AI upscaling tech for base PS5 in Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei
articles.content_orig:
Sony has announced QSSR - Quick Spectral Super Resolution - bringing PSSR-style AI upscaling to the base PS5 in a huge coup for existing console owners. Games need to be updated to add support for QSSR, but two are already ready: Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei.
It was thought to be impossible for PSSR to work on the base PS5, as it lacks the dedicated AI upscaling hardware necessary, but Sony has managed to bring a version of the technology to PS5 that is performant enough to be worth using - hence the "quick" part of the name.
We've already tested QSSR and early impressions are excellent - but how does this work, anyway?
In short, the firms used a more streamlined neural network architecture to fit into the PS5's limited hardware acceleration, and a hand-tuned implementation that trades off accuracy for performance. PSSR ought to always produce better-looking results, thanks to running on 300 TOPS of dedicated hardware in PS5 Pro, but QSSR should in turn outperform existing software-based upscaling and anti-aliasing solutions on the base PS5, like industry-standard TAA, Epic's Unreal Engine TSR and AMD's FSR 3 - especially when it comes to image stability.
Here's head of technology Mike Fitzgerald at Insomniac Games, developers of Marvel's Wolverine:
"QSSR adds more pixel-level clarity and stability to our environments, bringing out extra detail amidst the busy streets of Madripoor, the dense alleyways of Shinjuku, and many other areas across Logan's epic journey. It's a perfect companion to the launch of Marvel's Wolverine, and it brings a great taste of the PS5 Pro experience to our players on PS5."
And here's lead rendering engineer Jasmin Patry at Sucker Punch Productions, the studio behind Ghost of Yōtei:
"At Sucker Punch, we’re excited to bring QSSR to Ghost of Yōtei players so that they can experience the world we’ve created with even more clarity and detail. QSSR excels at resolving the fine details in our characters and environments and does so with a level of temporal stability that hasn’t been possible on the PS5 console until now. We’ve long wished that all PS5 players could experience the incredible image quality that PSSR brings to PS5 Pro, and QSSR is a positive step towards that goal!"
QSSR will be freely available for other PlayStation developers to implement now that it's officially been unveiled, and ought to be widely adopted. Any game with PSSR support can add QSSR support very easily, almost as a drop-in replacement that only requires some settings tweaks to suit the new level of performance.
Games that don't support PSSR can also be retrofitted with slightly more development work, and of course studios with upcoming PlayStation releases can also take QSSR into account much earlier in the development process to make full use of the tech. For example, I suspect the authors of Grand Theft Auto 6 could have just enough time to integrate QSSR if they so choose.
We have much more detail in our QSSR feature , based on several conversations with Sony engineers, so I'd encourage you to read that next if you haven't already.
What do you make of the news? Let me know in the comments below.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft makes Windows settings backup the default in 26H2
articles.title_zh: Microsoft makes Windows settings backup the default in 26H2
articles.content_orig:
Annual update installed. You're up to date, so nothing seems to have changed. Wait a minute...
Windows 11 26H2 is out, and Microsoft has enabled Windows settings backup by default, a move that could send administrators scrambling to opt out where they once had to opt in.
The latest release hasn't made a lot of shockwaves in the community featurewise. Users with up-to-date versions of 25H2 will unlikely notice much difference – 26H2 has the same code base, delivered via an enablement package. It even has the same set of known issues, although all are now "mitigated" in one way or another.
However, administrators will spot several important changes. The end-of-support clock is reset, and Microsoft has flipped some switches behind the scenes; notably, enabling Windows backup and restore (formerly Windows Backup for Organizations) by default.
The service, which was previously off by default, backs up a device's settings and a list of installed Microsoft Store apps. The idea is that when a user moves to a new device, a restore can happen during setup. Microsoft also listed an objective of the service as allowing "organizations to transition to a cloud-first approach for managing devices and user settings."
The problem is that many organizations are prohibited from sending this data to the cloud. As a result, the default-on setting won't apply in privacy-sensitive regions such as those covered by the EU Digital Markets Act, or in sovereign and restricted environments.
For many others running Windows 11 26H2, it'll now be enabled by default on eligible devices – Entra joined or Entra Hybrid joined. Unless an administrator has explicitly said no to the functionality, the act of installing the update will flip the switch, and the backups will begin.
Administrators will rightly be wary of anything that switches from opt-in to opt-out, even something so apparently useful and innocuous as a backup. Why wouldn't you want your users to be able to leap to a new device with ease? That assumes their data is also in the cloud, of course, since this only backs up settings and a list of Windows apps. Backing up data is something else entirely.
That is the real issue with the change. The release of Windows 11 26H2 isn't particularly exciting in itself, but flipping a long-standing opt-in to opt-out as part of it is likely to set more than a few nerves jangling. ®

articles.content_orig:
Visit Pokémon Trainer Central
World Space Week is almost here, and it’s never been better to be a fan of both the cosmos and Pokémon! The Pokémon Company International and the European Space Agency (ESA) have come together for an amazing collaboration to inspire the next generation of explorers.
Whether or not you see your future in the stars, you can take home a bit of that excitement starting today with a suite of collaboration items on PokemonCenter.com, including some other space-themed selections only available on the Pokémon Center’s US website.
You’ve seen plenty of Pikachu plush but have you ever seen one that’s traveled to outer space? Well...these Astronaut Pikachu Plush didn’t actually make the trip, but the white-suited Pikachu is just the same as the one French astronaut Sophie Adenot took to the International Space Station! You can bring home either a male Pikachu in a white spacesuit or female Pikachu in a blue flight suit—or both for a whole at-home crew!
If you’ve been wondering how to show off your enthusiasm for both Pokémon and space through your daily wardrobe, look no further than the Pokémon Center × ESA T-shirt, pullover hoodie, and bomber jacket. The shirt and hoodie feature the collaboration’s astronomically adorable main visual, and the bomber jacket boasts the same star Pokémon as stylish patches!
Looking for something a bit more subtle? The Pokémon Center × ESA pin and patch set have you covered with the same featured Pokémon and artwork. If being the envy of your local Pokémon TCG community is more your style, you can add an extra spacey touch to your next battle with a double deck box, card sleeves, and playmat.  We can’t forget about the binder either—your collection’s style is certain to be airtight.
